items.title: What are the strategies to minimise blood loss in major surgery?
items.sub: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.eyebrow: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.q: What are the strategies to minimise blood loss in major surgery?
items.a:
- Apply PBM before, during and after surgery: diagnose/treat anaemia, plan antithrombotics, meticulous haemostasis, appropriate minimally invasive technique, avoid hypothermia, use indicated TXA and selected cell salvage.
- Limit dilution and phlebotomy; use physiological and evidence-based transfusion decisions.
- ANH is selective: a 2025 large CPB trial did not reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs overall.
- Include consent, equipment/staff readiness and postoperative bleeding review.

items.title: How does cell salvage work?
items.sub: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.eyebrow: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.q: How does cell salvage work?
items.a:
- Shed blood mixes with manufacturer-specified anticoagulant, passes a reservoir filter and is centrifuged.
- Washing with IV-grade isotonic saline discards plasma, free Hb and most contaminants; labelled concentrated RBCs are returned through the appropriate filter.
- It supplies negligible platelets/factors, so major haemorrhage still needs haemostatic support.
- Use low suction, trained operators, traceability and the device expiry; avoid pressurising salvage bags.

items.title: What are the contraindications to cell salvage?
items.sub: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.eyebrow: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.q: What are the contraindications to cell salvage?
items.a:
- Avoid collecting gross faeces, urine, pus, antiseptic, topical haemostatic agents or unset cement.
- Sepsis and malignancy are relative, context-dependent cautions rather than universal absolute exclusions; washing/selected filters do not guarantee sterility or complete tumour-cell removal.
- Obstetric use requires a protocol and RhD assessment.
- Sickle disease/trait needs specialist evaluation.
- Respect the patient’s individual consent and accepted circuit configuration.

items.title: What are the advantages of cell salvage?
items.sub: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.eyebrow: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.q: What are the advantages of cell salvage?
items.a:
- Cell salvage reduces donor RBC exposure and conserves scarce/antibody-compatible blood, particularly in substantial blood loss.
- It returns the patient’s oxygen-carrying cells without donor storage, and can support some patients declining allogeneic blood.
- Benefits depend on usable yield and trained staffing; it does not replace platelets/factors, eliminate all transfusion risks or guarantee improved mortality.

items.title: How would you justify introducing cell salvage?
items.sub: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.eyebrow: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.q: How would you justify introducing cell salvage?
items.a:
- Audit case mix, blood loss, donor units, antibody/refusal cases and expected salvage yield.
- Compare equipment, disposables, maintenance and training/out-of-hours staffing with potential donor savings.
- Establish governance, selection/contamination protocols, consent, traceability and competencies.
- Pilot and audit donor exposure, yield, waste, costs and adverse events.
- Avoid promising automatic financial break-even or survival benefit.

items.title: What does point-of-care testing offer in major haemorrhage?
items.q: What does point-of-care testing offer in major haemorrhage?
items.a:
- Blood gas/Hb and ionised calcium give rapid physiological information; VEM provides whole-blood clot initiation, strength and lysis patterns that can guide targeted products.
- Early amplitudes are quicker than complete tracings.
- Limitations include expertise, cost, device-specific triggers, assay temperature, limited endothelial/platelet-drug representation and poor exclusion of DOAC effect.
- Continue conventional tests and source control; a normal tracing does not rule out clinically important bleeding.

items.title: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.sub: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.eyebrow: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.q: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.a:
- TXA is a lysine analogue that blocks plasminogen/plasmin binding to fibrin and reduces fibrinolysis.
- It stabilises formed clot rather than supplying factors or raising platelet count.
- Benefit depends on indication and timing: trauma and postpartum haemorrhage have time-critical evidence, while GI bleeding does not share the same benefit.
- Dose and renal adjustment follow the relevant local pathway.

items.title: What are the adverse effects of tranexamic acid?
items.sub: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.eyebrow: Reducing blood loss and tranexamic acid
items.q: What are the adverse effects of tranexamic acid?
items.a:
- Rapid IV dosing can cause hypotension; seizures are dose-related, especially with high-dose cardiac regimens or renal accumulation.
- Consider thrombosis history, interactions and context; safety cannot be assumed from absence of statistical significance.
- POISE-3 reduced bleeding but did not establish prespecified cardiovascular noninferiority.
- TRACTION 2026 supports a noncardiac policy reducing RBC transfusion with VTE noninferiority on its specified margin, a different endpoint.
- TXA is not routine treatment for every haemorrhage.

items.title: How do you manage a Jehovah's Witness for major surgery?
items.sub: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.eyebrow: Cell salvage and refusal of blood
items.q: How do you manage a Jehovah's Witness for major surgery?
items.a:
- Discuss privately and document decision-making capacity, informed refusal and precisely which components/fractions or autologous circuits are accepted.
- Do not infer acceptance from religion alone.
- Optimise anaemia, plan surgery and senior multidisciplinary support, appropriate TXA/salvage and meticulous haemostasis; minimise sampling and dilution.
- Agree emergency limits, postoperative care and advance directives.
- Competent adult refusal remains relevant during unconsciousness; children or uncertainty require jurisdiction-specific senior/legal advice.

items.title: What is the difference between FFP, cryoprecipitate and PCC?
items.q: What is the difference between FFP, cryoprecipitate and PCC?
items.a:
- FFP supplies a broad range of coagulation factors in a substantial volume, commonly 15–20 mL/kg when indicated.
- Cryo primarily supplies fibrinogen plus FVIII/VWF/FXIII; NZ high-fibrinogen apheresis units are not interchangeable with overseas pools.
- Four-factor PCC supplies II, VII, IX and X in low volume, principally for rapid vitamin-K antagonist reversal with vitamin K.
- It contains little/no useful fibrinogen and is not a universal plasma substitute.
- All have risks and need reassessment.

items.title: How do you ensure safe administration of blood in theatre?
items.q: How do you ensure safe administration of blood in theatre?
items.a:
- Confirm indication/consent and special requirements; perform bedside patient/product identity and compatibility checks according to local policy.
- Inspect expiry/integrity, use an approved filter/warmer and dedicated compatible line, and record baseline observations.
- NZBS recommends 0.9% saline for priming/flushing/co-mixing blood components.
- Monitor closely, especially initially, document traceability and respond promptly to reactions.
- Do not heat blood above 41°C.

items.title: How long can red cells be out of the blood fridge?
items.q: How long can red cells be out of the blood fridge?
items.a:
- Keep RBCs in validated monitored storage at 2–6°C until needed.
- Start promptly, ordinarily within 30 minutes of removal; if delayed, consult the blood bank about safe return rather than storing in an unvalidated theatre fridge.
- Complete transfusion within the applicable four-hour limit.
- Validated transport systems may have different controlled arrangements.
- These rules do not apply unchanged to platelets, plasma, cryo or salvaged RBCs.

items.title: How do you diagnose a transfusion reaction under anaesthesia?
items.q: How do you diagnose a transfusion reaction under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Suspect a reaction with otherwise unexplained hypotension, bronchospasm, rash, fever, rising airway pressure/hypoxaemia, haemoglobinuria or diffuse bleeding; anaesthesia can hide symptoms.
- Stop the unit, call for help and blood-bank advice, support ABC and check identity.
- Keep IV access using fresh tubing/normal saline; save bag/tubing and send directed samples.
- Assess haemolysis, sepsis, anaphylaxis, TRALI/TACO and other causes concurrently.

items.title: What do you do for a suspected acute haemolytic reaction?
items.q: What do you do for a suspected acute haemolytic reaction?
items.a:
- Stop transfusion immediately; check patient/unit identity and alert the blood bank.
- Support oxygenation, circulation and renal perfusion with monitored resuscitation, treating shock and DIC.
- Send repeat compatibility/DAT, haemolysis and coagulation samples and urine, returning the unit/tubing.
- Monitor potassium, renal function and urine output.
- Do not routinely force diuresis with furosemide/mannitol in a shocked patient; treat physiology and obtain specialist advice.

items.title: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
items.q: How do you distinguish TRALI from TACO?
items.a:
- Both cause acute hypoxaemia and pulmonary oedema and can overlap.
- TRALI is permeability oedema beginning during/within six hours, without hydrostatic oedema as the main explanation; fever/hypotension may occur.
- TACO is circulatory overload during/within twelve hours, supported by fluid balance, cardiac findings and response to diuresis.
- BNP, hypertension or echo alone are not definitive.
- Stop transfusion, support ventilation; diurese TACO as appropriate, but avoid routine diuresis for hypovolaemic TRALI.

items.title: What is the definition of massive transfusion?
items.q: What is the definition of massive transfusion?
items.a:
- Historical massive transfusion is ≥10 RBC units in 24 hours or replacement of a blood volume.
- These retrospective definitions can miss early exsanguination.
- Activate a major haemorrhage protocol from ongoing critical bleeding, physiological shock and predicted need, rather than waiting for a numerical threshold.
- Communicate cause, urgency and trajectory and reassess frequently.

items.title: What ratio of products is used in massive transfusion?
items.q: What ratio of products is used in massive transfusion?
items.a:
- Use the local MHP with balanced initial components, then targeted therapy when tests and clinical response are available.
- Ratios must specify component equivalence: one adult platelet dose is not one donor unit or one bag of every product.
- Australian guidance gives minimum plasma one per two RBCs and one adult platelet dose per eight RBCs, with early delivery according to severity.
- PROPPR favoured haemostasis/exsanguination outcomes for 1:1:1 but did not establish an overall mortality advantage.
- Ensure fibrinogen and calcium are addressed.

items.title: What are the metabolic complications of massive transfusion?
items.q: What are the metabolic complications of massive transfusion?
items.a:
- Watch hypothermia, citrate-related hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia, hyperkalaemia, acid–base disturbance and later citrate-associated alkalosis.
- Coagulopathy, volume overload, pulmonary reactions, identification errors and infection also matter.
- Use approved warming, rapid serial blood gas/electrolytes, ECG and haemostatic tests, replace deficits and avoid excessive empiric components after control.
- Treat the shock producing acidosis; do not assume every disturbance comes only from stored blood.

items.title: Why is the haemoglobin trigger flexible?
items.q: Why is the haemoglobin trigger flexible?
items.a:
- Hb is one part of oxygen delivery: consider bleeding trajectory, perfusion, ischaemia, cardiopulmonary reserve and physiological compensation.
- In stable adults, restrictive thresholds around 70 g/L often apply, with selected 75 cardiac/80 orthopaedic or CVD thresholds.
- Acute MI has distinct 2025 guidance favouring a conditional liberal strategy below 100 g/L with low certainty.
- Active haemorrhage and brain injury need separate assessment.
- A higher oxygen requirement may justify a higher, not lower, Hb transfusion threshold.

items.title: What are the compensatory responses to anaemia?
items.q: What are the compensatory responses to anaemia?
items.a:
- Lower viscosity and reduced oxygen content trigger increased cardiac output, sympathetic activation and redistribution of flow, with greater tissue oxygen extraction.
- Chronic anaemia increases 2,3-DPG and shifts the dissociation curve right; these responses are not instantaneous in acute bleeding.
- Compensation is limited by coronary/valvular disease, beta blockade, age or hypovolaemia.
- Oxygen delivery remains CO × arterial oxygen content, dominated by Hb-bound oxygen.

items.title: What did TRICC and FOCUS show?
items.q: What did TRICC and FOCUS show?
items.a:
- TRICC supported a restrictive strategy in selected haemodynamically stable ICU patients; it was not an acute-haemorrhage or acute-MI rule.
- FOCUS found no functional/mortality advantage to a liberal 100 g/L strategy over restrictive/symptom-based transfusion in high-risk patients after hip-fracture surgery.
- Both require population and exclusions to be stated; neither proves that every patient should wait until 70 g/L regardless of ischaemia.

items.title: What are the risks of allogeneic transfusion?
items.q: What are the risks of allogeneic transfusion?
items.a:
- Acute risks include haemolysis, febrile/allergic/anaphylactic reactions, bacterial sepsis, TRALI, TACO and metabolic complications.
- Delayed risks include alloimmunisation, delayed haemolysis/hyperhaemolysis, iron overload and selected TA-GVHD/infections.
- Leukodepletion does not replace irradiation when indicated.
- Explain absolute risk using current local haemovigilance rather than one universal infection number, and balance these risks against harm from untreated anaemia/haemorrhage.

items.title: What are the perioperative problems of sickle cell disease?
items.q: What are the perioperative problems of sickle cell disease?
items.a:
- SCD causes haemolytic anaemia, vaso-occlusive pain, acute chest syndrome and multiorgan injury; consider renal/cardiopulmonary disease, stroke, transfusion antibodies and chronic therapy.
- Avoid hypoxaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, acidosis, pain and prolonged stasis without causing fluid overload.
- Coordinate analgesia, respiratory care, VTE prophylaxis and a haematology transfusion plan.
- HbSC and sickle β-thalassaemia may have important disease despite a higher baseline Hb.

items.title: What is the role of exchange transfusion in sickle cell disease?
items.q: What is the role of exchange transfusion in sickle cell disease?
items.a:
- Exchange lowers HbS without an excessive rise in viscosity and is considered for severe disease, high-risk surgery or a baseline Hb too high for simple transfusion.
- ASH suggests individualised preoperative transfusion for operations under GA lasting over one hour, rather than universal exchange.
- A typical postoperative Hb range is 90–110 g/L; HbS <30% is reserved for selected high-risk settings, not every case.
- Consider alloimmunisation, compatible matching and delayed hyperhaemolysis.

items.title: What is the key airway feature of thalassaemia major?
items.q: What is the key airway feature of thalassaemia major?
items.a:
- Marrow expansion can cause maxillary prominence and facial changes, potentially complicating mask fit/intubation, but airway assessment must be individual.
- Other major issues are chronic anaemia, transfusional iron overload with cardiac/endocrine/liver disease, antibodies, splenectomy-related sepsis/thrombosis and chelation effects.
- Thalassaemia trait differs greatly from transfusion-dependent disease; do not reduce the condition to one airway sign.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues in haematological malignancy?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues in haematological malignancy?
items.a:
- Assess anaemia, thrombocytopenia/qualitative dysfunction, neutropenic infection and both bleeding and thrombosis.
- Consider tumour lysis with K/phosphate/uric-acid changes, hyperviscosity/leukostasis, DIC in APL, mediastinal masses and bone disease.
- Review chemotherapy-related cardiac/pulmonary/renal injury, steroids and interactions.
- Coordinate counts/products and infection management with haematology; irradiated RBC requirements depend on diagnosis/treatment, not every malignancy.
- NZ platelets are routinely irradiated.

items.title: How do you manage ITP before splenectomy?
items.q: How do you manage ITP before splenectomy?
items.a:
- Confirm ITP and exclude other causes; coordinate a target count and haemostasis plan with haematology/surgery.
- Steroids and/or IVIG can raise platelets; TPO agonists may be useful when time permits.
- Platelet transfusion is short-lived but appropriate for major bleeding or urgent surgical support, timed with therapy/procedure rather than categorically withheld.
- Plan postsplenectomy infection prevention, immunisation and thromboprophylaxis, and monitor for postoperative thrombocytosis/thrombosis.

items.title: How do HbC, HbE and sickle variants change the haemoglobinopathy overview?
items.q: How do HbC, HbE and sickle variants change the haemoglobinopathy overview?
items.a:
- Sickle variants include HbSS, HbSC and sickle β-thalassaemia, with different anaemia and vaso-occlusive phenotypes.
- HbC disease can cause haemolysis, while HbSC carries sickling risk.
- HbE trait is usually mild but HbE/β-thalassaemia can be severe. α/β-thalassaemia range from trait to transfusion-dependent disease.
- Identify the genotype, phenotype and organ/transfusion history.
- G6PD deficiency is an enzymopathy rather than a structural haemoglobinopathy.

items.title: What do the recent ANH and transfusion trials change?
items.q: What do the recent ANH and transfusion trials change?
items.a:
- The 2025 multicentre CPB ANH trial did not significantly reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs; selected use needs a realistic indication.
- FIBRES found fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate for component use after cardiac surgery, not the reverse.
- TRAIN and HEMOTION studied different acute-brain-injury populations/thresholds and had different primary results.
- Quote population, intervention, endpoint and uncertainty rather than applying one threshold to all patients.

items.title: What do ROTEM LI30, ML and TEG LY30 mean?
items.q: What do ROTEM LI30, ML and TEG LY30 mean?
items.a:
- ROTEM LI30 is the percentage of clot firmness remaining 30 minutes after clotting time; a lower value indicates more lysis.
- ROTEM maximum lysis is percentage loss from maximum firmness; higher means more lysis.
- TEG LY30 is percentage amplitude loss 30 minutes after maximum amplitude.
- Their direction and time reference differ.
- Check platform/reagent/local reference limits rather than transferring one numerical trigger to another.

items.title: When is PCC inappropriate despite a prolonged VEM clotting time?
items.q: When is PCC inappropriate despite a prolonged VEM clotting time?
items.a:
- First check fibrinogen, anticoagulants/heparin, sampling, temperature and the clinical bleeding context.
- Severe low fibrinogen can prolong clotting time and must be corrected.
- PCC does not replace fibrinogen or platelets and may cause thrombosis; empirical routine PCC for all trauma is unsupported.
- Use a validated local algorithm and reassess rather than treating one tracing in isolation.

items.title: How do you recognise and initially manage acute limb ischaemia?
items.q: How do you recognise and initially manage acute limb ischaemia?
items.a:
- Sudden pain, pallor, coolness, absent pulses, paraesthesia or weakness require urgent vascular assessment; neurological loss indicates threatened viability.
- Document perfusion and Doppler signals, give analgesia and systemic UFH unless contraindicated, and arrange urgent imaging/revascularisation without delaying rescue.
- After reperfusion monitor potassium, acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, AKI and compartment syndrome.
- Treat the embolic/thrombotic source and plan ongoing antithrombotics.

items.title: How does regional citrate anticoagulation differ from systemic heparin?
items.q: How does regional citrate anticoagulation differ from systemic heparin?
items.a:
- Citrate chelates circuit calcium and usually needs separate calcium replacement and protocolised circuit/systemic ionised calcium, total calcium and acid–base monitoring.
- It does not provide systemic VTE treatment.
- Impaired citrate metabolism can cause falling systemic calcium, rising calcium needs, an increased total-to-ionised calcium ratio and acidosis.
- Heparin anticoagulates the patient and circuit, with bleeding/HIT risks.
- Select the strategy to the patient and local expertise.

items.title: What causes apparent heparin resistance?
items.q: What causes apparent heparin resistance?
items.a:
- Check dose delivery, sampling and the assay before escalation.
- High FVIII/fibrinogen can shorten APTT despite therapeutic heparin activity, whereas low antithrombin can reduce heparin effect; ACT is also affected by temperature, platelets and haemodilution.
- Compare a suitable anti-Xa assay and clinical circuit/thrombotic findings.
- Clarify assay antithrombin supplementation with the laboratory and seek specialist treatment rather than chasing one number.

items.title: How do you investigate an isolated prolonged APTT?
items.q: How do you investigate an isolated prolonged APTT?
items.a:
- First check sample quality, heparin contamination and anticoagulant exposure.
- A mixing study that corrects suggests factor deficiency; persistent or time-dependent noncorrection suggests an inhibitor, but drug effects complicate interpretation.
- Assess actual bleeding and measure relevant factors/inhibitor assays with haematology.
- Lupus anticoagulant may cause thrombosis rather than bleeding; factor XII deficiency can prolong APTT without a bleeding phenotype.

items.title: What suggests acquired haemophilia A?
items.q: What suggests acquired haemophilia A?
items.a:
- New spontaneous extensive skin/muscle or mucosal bleeding in a patient without lifelong/family bleeding, with isolated APTT prolongation and low FVIII, suggests an acquired inhibitor.
- Exclude anticoagulants and arrange incubated mixing/FVIII/inhibitor testing urgently.
- Control bleeding using specialist haemostatic therapy and eradicate the inhibitor with immunosuppression.
- Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and do not assume ordinary FVIII replacement will work with a high inhibitor titre.

items.title: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia a haemostatic emergency?
items.q: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia a haemostatic emergency?
items.a:
- APL can cause severe DIC and hyperfibrinolysis with catastrophic bleeding and thrombosis.
- Urgently involve haematology, obtain film/coagulation/fibrinogen trends and support platelets/fibrinogen according to the specialist pathway.
- Start disease-specific treatment promptly when suspected under haematology direction.
- Avoid nonessential invasive procedures and do not treat this as uncomplicated isolated thrombocytopenia.

items.title: What is your first approach to unexplained ICU anaemia?
items.q: What is your first approach to unexplained ICU anaemia?
items.a:
- Confirm the trend and sampling, assess physiology and exclude occult surgical/GI/retroperitoneal bleeding.
- Consider phlebotomy, haemodilution, haemolysis, inflammation/low erythropoietin, renal failure, deficiencies and marrow suppression.
- Use reticulocytes, film and directed tests.
- Treat the cause, conserve sampling and use population-appropriate transfusion decisions; do not give iron or RBCs reflexively.

items.title: When do you transfuse platelets in a nonbleeding patient?
items.q: When do you transfuse platelets in a nonbleeding patient?
items.a:
- Use the cause and procedure rather than one universal threshold.
- AABB/ICTMG 2025 recommends <10 ×10⁹/L for nonbleeding hypoproliferative chemotherapy/allogeneic transplant; selected ICU consumptive settings are conditional.
- Major nonneuraxial surgery generally uses <50, lumbar puncture <20, and compressible-site CVC <10.
- These are not neuraxial-anaesthesia thresholds.
- HIT/TTP/ITP require disease-specific judgment, particularly without bleeding.

items.title: How do DIC and TTP differ?
items.q: How do DIC and TTP differ?
items.a:
- DIC usually accompanies systemic illness with consumption, high D-dimer and often prolonged PT; fibrinogen may initially be high in sepsis.
- TTP produces thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolysis, usually without marked PT/APTT prolongation; neurological/renal findings vary.
- Send ADAMTS13 before treatment where possible, but urgent treatment must not await the result: haematology-led plasma exchange plus corticosteroids for suspected immune TTP, with caplacizumab/rituximab considered under the specialist pathway.
- Routine platelet transfusion is avoided in TTP except life-threatening bleeding or an essential procedure.

items.title: What suggests delayed haemolysis or hyperhaemolysis after transfusion?
items.q: What suggests delayed haemolysis or hyperhaemolysis after transfusion?
items.a:
- Days to weeks after transfusion, falling Hb, jaundice, dark urine and rising haemolysis markers suggest delayed immune haemolysis; antibodies may have been historically undetectable.
- In SCD, hyperhaemolysis can lower Hb below the pretransfusion value and may occur without a positive DAT.
- Involve haematology/blood bank urgently: further transfusion can worsen it and needs specialist justification/matching and treatment.

items.title: Which blood products require irradiation?
items.q: Which blood products require irradiation?
items.a:
- Irradiation prevents transfusion-associated GVHD from donor lymphocytes; it does not replace leukodepletion, CMV strategies or pathogen screening.
- RBC indications include selected lymphoid disease/treatments, cellular transplantation and certain donor relationships; follow current blood-bank guidance.
- Not every malignancy or haemoglobinopathy requires irradiated RBCs.
- NZ platelets are routinely irradiated.
- Consider RBC expiry/potassium and urgency with the blood bank.

items.title: What if emergency RBC compatibility is delayed by antibodies?
items.q: What if emergency RBC compatibility is delayed by antibodies?
items.a:
- Explain urgency to a senior blood-bank clinician/scientist, send correct samples and historical antibody details and control bleeding.
- Group O avoids ABO incompatibility but may still carry a relevant non-ABO antigen.
- The blood bank selects emergency-release blood when delay would be more dangerous.
- Warm autoantibodies can make every crossmatch reactive; seek underlying alloantibodies and best matching without withholding lifesaving transfusion for perfect serological compatibility.

items.title: How does FiiRST-2 differ from FARES-II and PROCOAG?
items.q: How does FiiRST-2 differ from FARES-II and PROCOAG?
items.a:
- FiiRST-2 compared an early FC-plus-PCC replacement package with frozen plasma in a trauma MHP and did not show superiority for 24-hour component use.
- FARES-II favoured PCC over plasma for haemostatic effectiveness in selected bleeding cardiac-surgery patients.
- PROCOAG did not support empirical adjunct PCC in trauma and found more thromboembolism.
- The deficit, population, comparator and endpoint matter; these trials do not support one universal PCC rule.

> **Closing point:** Do not merge distinct factor-replacement questions.

items.title: Why can normal APTT mislead in a haemophilia patient on new prophylaxis?
items.q: Why can normal APTT mislead in a haemophilia patient on new prophylaxis?
items.a:
- Emicizumab can normalise APTT and distort APTT-based FVIII/inhibitor tests without restoring endogenous FVIII.
- Use the haemophilia laboratory’s validated assays, including bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII where appropriate.
- Other non-factor drugs rebalance antithrombin/TFPI pathways and need their own assessment, monitoring and rescue plan.
- Major surgery and neuraxial safety cannot be cleared by APTT alone.

> **Closing point:** Name the drug before choosing the assay or haemostatic rescue.

items.title: What makes mechanical-valve pregnancy anticoagulation different from ordinary VTE?
items.q: What makes mechanical-valve pregnancy anticoagulation different from ordinary VTE?
items.a:
- Effective valve protection is essential; DOACs are not an alternative.
- VKA gives reliable maternal protection but crosses the placenta; no fetal dose is proven safe.
- If LMWH is chosen, use a specialist therapeutic twice-daily regimen with anti-Xa monitoring, not a standard prophylaxis prescription.
- Plan gestation, delivery transition, neuraxial constraints and postpartum restart with the Pregnancy Heart Team.

> **Closing point:** The maternal and fetal risks change with stage and regimen.

items.title: What is the TXA clock and dose for treating postpartum haemorrhage?
items.q: What is the TXA clock and dose for treating postpartum haemorrhage?
items.a:
- WHO: 1 g IV over ten minutes as soon as possible, within three hours of birth.
- Repeat 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.
- It accompanies source control/uterotonics and resuscitation; do not wait for a VEM lysis signal.
- Treatment evidence does not justify routine prophylaxis for every birth; keep TXA away from neuraxial drugs.

> **Closing point:** Count from birth and prevent wrong-route administration.

items.title: How should you answer the historical aprotinin debate today?
items.q: How should you answer the historical aprotinin debate today?
items.a:
- Discuss efficacy against bleeding/transfusion alongside renal, thrombotic and allergy concerns.
- The 2007 report predates BART (2008); distinguish historical evidence from later safety data.
- Selected European use is restricted to high-bleeding-risk isolated on-pump CABG; verify local licence and alternatives.
- A restricted approval is not a mandate for all CPB procedures or proof of NZ access.

> **Closing point:** Give a dated, population-specific benefit–risk conclusion.

items.title: When should you suspect HLH in ICU?
items.q: When should you suspect HLH in ICU?
items.a:
- Persistent fever, falling counts and a markedly high/rising ferritin with organ dysfunction should trigger an HLH assessment, especially when expected improvement with sepsis treatment does not occur.
- Check fibrinogen, triglycerides, liver tests and HScore with specialist input.
- Ferritin alone is not diagnostic; marrow haemophagocytosis is neither required nor specific.
- Infection and HLH can coexist.

items.title: What are the immediate treatment priorities in probable HLH?
items.q: What are the immediate treatment priorities in probable HLH?
items.a:
- Support failing organs, continue indicated antimicrobials and call the specialist team.
- Treat hyperinflammation and investigate/treat triggers in parallel.
- Glucocorticoids, anakinra and/or IVIg are context-dependent initial options; selected cases need etoposide or other directed therapy.
- Avoid delaying treatment for every diagnostic result.
- Follow counts, ferritin, fibrinogen and organ response.

items.title: What must a peripartum anticoagulation plan specify?
items.q: What must a peripartum anticoagulation plan specify?
items.a:
- Indication and exact drug/dose, renal function, instructions for labour and planned delivery, last-dose timing, neuraxial alternatives, catheter removal and restart ownership.
- Restart requires haemostasis and the applicable neuraxial intervals.
- Low-dose prophylaxis after previous VTE is not treatment of acute PE or a mechanical valve; any UFH switch is an individual decision.

items.title: What do Highlow and intermediate-dose LMWH mean for neuraxial planning?
items.q: What do Highlow and intermediate-dose LMWH mean for neuraxial planning?
items.a:
- Highlow did not demonstrate better recurrent-VTE prevention with intermediate than low-dose prophylaxis in its prior-VTE pregnancy population.
- Higher dosing can reduce neuraxial access after unplanned labour.
- There is insufficient evidence for one precise intermediate-dose 12–24-hour interval; seek the actual-dose/local specialist plan.
- Do not extrapolate to acute-VTE or mechanical-valve under-treatment.

items.title: How do you distinguish CAR-T CRS from ICANS?
items.q: How do you distinguish CAR-T CRS from ICANS?
items.a:
- CRS typically causes fever with hypoxia/hypotension; treat possible infection concurrently, support organs and use the CAR-T centre grading/treatment pathway, including tocilizumab when indicated.
- ICANS causes language, attention, handwriting or consciousness change and seizures.
- Assess ICE score, exclude mimics and obtain neurological/ICU help.
- Steroids are central for significant ICANS; tocilizumab alone is not treatment of isolated ICANS.

items.title: What IVIg safety points matter in haematology?
items.q: What IVIg safety points matter in haematology?
items.a:
- Confirm indication, product, total grams and dosing weight; follow the product-specific infusion chart and distinguish g/kg dose from mL/kg/hour rate.
- Watch for infusion reactions/anaphylaxis, thrombosis, AKI, aseptic meningitis and haemolysis/positive DAT.
- Assess fluid, renal and thrombotic risk.
- An IgG product is not risk-free or interchangeable with platelets.

items.title: What suggests post-transfusion purpura?
items.q: What suggests post-transfusion purpura?
items.a:
- Profound thrombocytopenia with bleeding about 5–12 days after cellular transfusion, often in someone previously sensitised by pregnancy/transfusion.
- Recipient anti-HPA responses cause donor and bystander platelet destruction.
- Notify blood bank/haematology, test HPA antibodies and use specialist IVIg.
- Avoid routine random-donor platelets; life-threatening bleeding needs selected support and future product planning.

items.title: How does VITT differ from ITP or ordinary HIT?
items.q: How does VITT differ from ITP or ordinary HIT?
items.a:
- VITT is an exposure-linked anti-PF4 syndrome with thrombocytopenia and thrombosis, often at unusual sites, high D-dimer and sometimes low fibrinogen.
- Send PF4 ELISA and symptom-directed imaging; rapid HIT tests may miss it.
- With strong suspicion, involve haematology for prompt IVIg and non-heparin anticoagulation while results are pending.
- Avoid routine platelets; catastrophic bleeding is an individual exception.

items.title: How do primary haemostasis and the cell-based stages of secondary haemostasis work?
items.q: How do primary haemostasis and the cell-based stages of secondary haemostasis work?
items.a: **Primary haemostasis:** vessel injury exposes collagen and vWF; platelets adhere through **GPIb–vWF**, activate via ADP/thromboxane/thrombin and aggregate through **GPIIb/IIIa–fibrinogen**. **Secondary haemostasis:** tissue factor–VIIa initiates small amounts of thrombin; amplification activates platelets and cofactors V/VIII/XI; propagation on activated platelet surfaces produces the **thrombin burst** via tenase (IXa–VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa–Va). Thrombin generates fibrin; **factor XIIIa cross-links** it. Platelet/vWF defects typically cause mucosal/immediate oozing, factor defects deeper/delayed bleeding. PT/APTT assess limited pathways and can be normal despite clinically important bleeding.

items.title: How do natural anticoagulants and fibrinolysis prevent uncontrolled clotting?
items.q: How do natural anticoagulants and fibrinolysis prevent uncontrolled clotting?
items.a: **Antithrombin** inhibits thrombin (IIa) and Xa; heparin potentiates it. Activated **protein C with protein S** inactivates Va and VIIIa; **TFPI** limits the tissue factor–VIIa pathway. Endothelial **tPA** converts plasminogen to **plasmin**, which degrades fibrin (including cross-linked fibrin, producing D-dimer). **PAI-1** inhibits plasminogen activation and **α₂-antiplasmin** neutralises free plasmin. Haemostasis depends on the balance between thrombin generation and fibrinolysis: derangements can produce both haemorrhage and thrombosis, and a normal PT/APTT does not establish normal in-vivo haemostasis.

items.title: What is the RBC storage lesion, and should we routinely request fresh blood?
items.q: What is the RBC storage lesion, and should we routinely request fresh blood?
items.a: Stored RBCs show **falling 2,3-DPG**, reduced deformability and membrane changes, **extracellular potassium accumulation**, acid–base/metabolic changes and release of free haemoglobin/microparticles. These biochemical changes do **not** establish that standard-issue RBCs cause worse clinical outcomes: major adult randomised trials have not supported routinely requesting the freshest available units. Discuss product age/processing with the blood bank in selected neonatal or paediatric transfusions, exchange transfusion, very rapid/high-volume transfusion or other special settings. Follow validated storage, warming and administration policy rather than using a blanket 'fresh blood' rule.

items.title: What is transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM), and why is its significance uncertain?
items.q: What is transfusion-related immunomodulation (TRIM), and why is its significance uncertain?
items.a: **TRIM** denotes possible changes in recipient immune responses after exposure to donor blood components, potentially involving donor leukocytes, soluble mediators and inflammatory signalling. Older observational studies linked transfusion to postoperative infection and cancer recurrence, but illness severity, surgery and transfusion indication strongly **confound causal interpretation**; modern leukodepletion changes exposure. TRIM is **not a distinct acute reaction** with a diagnostic assay or specific antidote. Limit unnecessary allogeneic transfusion through PBM and use indicated component processing rather than claiming that transfusion inevitably causes immunosuppression or malignancy recurrence.

items.title: How do you recognise and manage methaemoglobinaemia?
items.q: How do you recognise and manage methaemoglobinaemia?
items.a:
Ferric **Fe³⁺** haemoglobin cannot carry oxygen normally and increases the affinity of remaining ferrous haem sites, reducing tissue oxygen delivery. Suspect it after oxidant exposure (**prilocaine/benzocaine**, dapsone or nitrites) with cyanosis or unexpectedly low pulse oximetry (often near 85%) **despite a relatively normal PaO₂**. Confirm with **multiwavelength co-oximetry**: standard pulse oximetry and calculated blood-gas saturation are unreliable. Stop the cause, give oxygen, support physiology and consult toxicology/critical care; give **methylene blue** for significant symptoms or concentrations under a supervised protocol, recognising reduced efficacy/haemolysis risk in **G6PD deficiency** and potential serotonin toxicity with serotonergic medicines. Alternative specialist measures may be required. This is a dys-haemoglobinaemia, **not** a structural globin-chain disorder.

> Supplementary dys-haemoglobinaemia differential (not a dedicated chapter in the Set 2 notes).

items.title: Why can myeloproliferative neoplasms produce both thrombosis and bleeding?
items.q: Why can myeloproliferative neoplasms produce both thrombosis and bleeding?
items.a: Polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia can cause **hyperviscosity, platelet activation and arterial/venous thrombosis**. Yet extreme thrombocytosis may remove high-molecular-weight vWF multimers, causing **acquired von Willebrand syndrome** and paradoxical mucosal/procedural bleeding; platelet number is not the same as platelet function. Preoperatively assess previous thrombosis/bleeding, count/haematocrit, drugs, and vWF activity when the phenotype or extreme platelet count suggests it. Coordinate cytoreduction/phlebotomy or antithrombotic and haemostatic treatment with haematology; tailor perioperative thromboprophylaxis and avoid assuming all patients should receive aspirin or platelets automatically.

items.title: 1. Reversal of warfarin, DOACs and heparin for urgent surgery
items.q: Discuss the options for reversal of warfarin, direct oral anticoagulants and heparin in a patient requiring urgent surgery.
items.a:
## Decide whether reversal is needed

Assess urgency, site/severity of bleeding, procedure, thrombotic indication, exact dose/time, CrCl, interactions and available drug-specific tests. Pause the drug and control the source. If a procedure can safely wait, clearance may be safer than reversal. Do not delay resuscitation of critical bleeding for a laboratory result. Normal PT/APTT does not exclude DOAC activity; calibrated anti-Xa for Xa drugs and dilute thrombin time/ecarin testing for dabigatran are more useful when available.

## Match reversal to the agent

| Drug | Urgent strategy | Important limits |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | **4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K** for life-threatening bleeding/urgent reversal; common protocol ranges PCC 25–50 IU/kg by INR/weight and vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slowly | Use current NZ Beriplex protocol, maximum doses and rate; recheck INR promptly and later. Vitamin K takes hours but sustains correction. FFP is a fallback if PCC unavailable, not required routinely with 4F-PCC |
| Dabigatran | **Idarucizumab 5 g IV**, two 2.5-g doses, for qualifying uncontrolled bleeding/urgent surgery | Renal failure can cause rebound; repeat appropriate assays/clinical review. Dialysis removes dabigatran but is slower/logistically difficult |
| Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban | For selected critical bleeding, specialist-directed **4F-PCC**, commonly 25–50 IU/kg under protocol | Off-label haemostatic support, not drug removal; thrombosis risk. Andexanet has restricted indications/availability, is not routine urgent-surgery reversal, and does not cover every Xa drug |
| UFH | Stop; **protamine ≈1 mg per 100 U recently administered**, reduce for elapsed time and use local maximum/rate | Slow administration; hypotension, anaphylaxis and pulmonary hypertension; excess protamine can impair haemostasis |
| Enoxaparin/LMWH | Protamine partly reverses; common example **1 mg per 1 mg enoxaparin if within 8 h**, lower dose later, further dose only with specialist review | Anti-Xa activity is incompletely reversed; renal dysfunction prolongs effect |
| Fondaparinux | Stop; supportive/source-directed care and specialist rescue decision | No specific antidote; do not routinely prescribe rFVIIa/PCC for every exposure |

**Andexanet update:** the FDA concluded serious thrombotic risks outweighed benefits; US commercial sales ended December 2025. This is not a statement about NZ stock. Check current local approval/availability. It can cause heparin unresponsiveness, an important problem before CPB. It should not be taught as universally preferred first-line reversal. Activated charcoal is an early-ingestion option with airway protection (usually around 2 h; later only drug-specific advice), not a blanket 8-hour rule.

## Support and restart

Maintain temperature, physiological iCa and perfusion; use RBCs/components for the actual deficit, and TXA for an appropriate indication. Plasma/platelets do not specifically neutralise a DOAC; normal VEM does not prove clearance. Avoid unsafe neuraxial techniques. Document repeat INR/drug assessment, source control, thrombotic surveillance and a plan to restart prophylactic or therapeutic anticoagulation when haemostasis permits; therapeutic restart is often later than prophylaxis after major surgery.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Related initiation decision: new postoperative AF

Starting anticoagulation for new postoperative AF is a separate question from reversing a pre-existing drug. Establish onset/duration, recurrence, stroke risk, the operation's bleeding consequences and achieved haemostasis. Treat acute physiological triggers with the cardiac/ICU team. Persistent or recurrent AF needs a documented decision on anticoagulation and follow-up; a brief apparently transient episode should not simply be forgotten. A duration such as 48 hours is not a universal command to anticoagulate a freshly bleeding patient, and a bleeding score alone is not an automatic veto. Agent, start time and duration need shared assessment, renal review and reassessment after recovery. Haemodynamic instability may require urgent cardioversion without waiting for a prolonged pre-anticoagulation schedule. Full arrhythmia management belongs to the cardiac set. [AF25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924001252)

## Self-marking checklist
- Defines critical bleeding/urgency and balances thrombosis
- Checks last dose, CrCl and appropriate assays
- Warfarin: 4F-PCC plus sustained vitamin K correction
- Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g and rebound assessment
- Xa drugs: qualified PCC/andexanet discussion, not universal first-line antidote
- UFH/LMWH protamine dosing and incomplete reversal
- Source control, supportive treatment and restart plan
- Separates postoperative-AF anticoagulation initiation from reversal, with haemostasis and follow-up

items.title: 2. Massive pulmonary embolism after hip replacement
items.q: A 60-year-old woman becomes acutely hypoxic and hypotensive on the second postoperative day after hip replacement. Discuss the diagnosis and management of massive pulmonary embolism.
items.a:
## Recognise and stabilise high-risk PE

Call senior help, PERT/cardiology, ICU and the surgeon. Postoperative hypoxaemia plus hypotension suggests cardiopulmonary failure but PE is not proven: exclude haemorrhage, MI, sepsis, tamponade, tension pneumothorax and fat embolism. Check perfusion, oxygenation, ECG, gas/lactate, Hb, renal function and bedside echo. RV dilation/strain supports PE but is neither specific nor always present; do not diagnose it from McConnell's sign alone. CTPA if transport is safe; do not send a collapsing patient away merely to complete the usual pathway. Postoperative D-dimer is usually unhelpful.

Provide oxygen, maintain RV coronary/systemic perfusion (often noradrenaline) and avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Give small fluid only if underfilled, with response assessment; RV volume loading can worsen output. Intubation may precipitate arrest: if unavoidable use an experienced team, reduced/titrated induction, pressor support and carefully managed ventilation. Consider inhaled pulmonary vasodilator as rescue, not definitive clot treatment.

## Anticoagulation and reperfusion

Anticoagulate promptly if bleeding risk permits. **2026 AHA/ACC guidance generally prefers LMWH over UFH when initial parenteral treatment is required**. In this shocked postoperative patient, need for rapid interruption/reversal, impending procedures or severe renal failure may justify UFH under the local protocol; do not describe UFH as mandatory for every PE. A common UFH VTE protocol is 80 U/kg bolus then 18 U/kg/h, but recent surgery/bleeding may modify or omit the bolus; titrate by the validated assay.

Persistent shock requires urgent advanced-treatment assessment. Major surgery 2 days ago is a **major contraindication to systemic thrombolysis**, not a trivial relative caution. Mechanical catheter thrombectomy or surgical embolectomy may be preferred if rapidly available; catheter thrombolysis still causes bleeding. In otherwise fatal collapse, systemic lysis may be a rescue after a documented multidisciplinary risk decision. Standard non-arrest alteplase treatment commonly uses 100 mg over 2 h; arrest regimens vary—follow the local ALS/PE protocol rather than claiming a universal bolus. Continue prolonged CPR after lysis when indicated under the arrest guideline. VA-ECMO may bridge selected refractory cases to definitive care, not replace it.

## Ongoing care

ICU monitoring, bleeding and RV reassessment, and a duration/agent plan (at least 3 months for most treated PE, longer with persistent risk). IVC filter only for a genuine anticoagulation contraindication or selected recurrence despite treatment, with retrieval follow-up. The 2026 categories A–E supplement older “massive/submassive” labels; persistent hypotensive failure is category E, requiring further clinical subclassification.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises shock and plausible alternative diagnoses
- Uses bedside echo and CTPA according to stability
- Protects RV perfusion and avoids harmful volume/ventilation
- Qualifies LMWH preference and selected UFH use
- Recognises major surgical bleeding contraindication to lysis
- Discusses catheter/surgical reperfusion and selected ECMO
- Plans ICU, anticoagulation duration and limited retrievable-filter use

items.title: 3. Suspected HIT after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient on day 7 of heparin after cardiac surgery has a platelet count that has fallen from 250 to 90 x 10^9/L and a new arterial thrombosis. Discuss the diagnosis and management, including implications for anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Probability and confirmation

The platelet fall is **64%**, with onset day 7 and new arterial thrombosis: a high-probability HIT pattern unless a strong competing explanation changes the score. **4Ts: 0–3 low, 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high**. Distinguish the expected early post-CPB fall/recovery from a second day-5–10 fall; PF4 antibodies are common after CPB and a positive immunoassay alone does not diagnose HIT. Send an IgG PF4 immunoassay and functional assay as appropriate, but do not wait to treat a high-probability case. Review sepsis, DIC, drugs and TMA.

## Immediate treatment

Stop **all heparin**, including flushes, LMWH and heparin-containing products/devices where relevant. Begin a **nonheparin anticoagulant** at treatment intensity for thrombosis unless bleeding dictates an individual plan: argatroban, bivalirudin, danaparoid, fondaparinux or a DOAC according to stability, organ function and availability. Argatroban needs major dose reduction with hepatic dysfunction/critical illness; bivalirudin needs renal adjustment. Use the agent-specific monitoring protocol; CPB doses differ markedly from routine ICU infusion doses.

Urgent vascular review for limb-threatening arterial occlusion; assess/screen for additional thrombosis. Avoid routine prophylactic platelets, but serious bleeding or an urgent intervention can justify them. Do not start warfarin until platelet recovery (usually ≥150 ×10⁹/L); reverse early warfarin with vitamin K if appropriate and plan specialist overlap/INR interpretation. Duration depends on isolated HIT versus HIT with thrombosis, often 3–6 months for HITT.

## Anaesthetic and future bypass implications

Document a clear HIT alert and timing/laboratory status. Defer nonurgent CPB during acute/subacute-A HIT until an appropriate phase if possible; urgent CPB often uses **bivalirudin in an experienced centre**, or specialist plasma-exchange/heparin strategies. Brief intraoperative heparin may be appropriate in subacute-B or remote HIT, with avoidance before/after and postoperative platelet surveillance; “wait until every antibody is negative” is too absolute. Avoid neuraxial techniques during active parenteral direct-thrombin inhibition; an assumed washout alone is not sufficient permission.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Calculates fall and applies correct 4Ts categories
- Distinguishes post-CPB antibodies from clinical HIT
- Stops all heparin and treats before delayed tests when indicated
- Selects nonheparin treatment by organ function and setting
- Treats limb thrombosis and looks for other events
- Avoids routine platelets/early warfarin with justified exceptions
- Explains acute versus remote HIT and CPB/regional implications

items.title: 4. Massive transfusion and protocol design
items.q: Discuss the principles and complications of massive transfusion, and how you would structure a massive transfusion protocol in your hospital.
items.a:
## Activate for critical bleeding, not a retrospective unit count

Historical definitions (>10 RBC units/24 h or one blood volume) describe exposure but are poor activation triggers. Use rapid ongoing loss, shock/perfusion, likely need for escalating blood and the local **major haemorrhage protocol (MHP)**. Call a leader, senior surgeon/anaesthetist, blood bank, runner and laboratory support; achieve surgical/IR haemostasis concurrently. Protect oxygen delivery, obtain large-bore access, warm the patient and use a validated rapid infuser. Blood refusal/special antibodies require immediate communication.

## Initial component support and monitoring

Use the local balanced pack while results are pending, then target deficits. State ratio order and adult platelet-dose equivalence: **1:1:1 is not one adult apheresis platelet bag for every RBC unit**. NBA guidance suggests at least 1 FFP per 2 RBC and 1 adult platelet dose per 8 RBC in ratio-based support; local trauma packs can target higher ratios. These are minimum delivery recommendations, not reasons to wait until the eighth unit. PROPPR did not show significant overall 24-h/30-day mortality superiority, but 1:1:1 improved haemostasis/early exsanguination outcomes.

Measure serial gas/Hb, iCa/K/Mg, lactate/pH, core temperature, platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and VEM, with repeat intervals set by bleeding speed and intervention (often 15–30 min during unstable loss). Maintain physiological iCa and normothermia. Use platelets commonly >50 ×10⁹/L (>100 for selected intracranial/critical-site bleeding), fibrinogen generally >1.5–2 g/L (obstetrics ≥2), and assay/local thresholds. Give TXA for the indicated population/time window; do not give routine empirical PCC or rFVIIa. Use appropriate emergency-release group O RBCs (O RhD-negative prioritised when needed), transition to group-specific/compatible stock under blood-bank policy; do not prescribe O-negative for every adult indefinitely.

## Prevent and respond to complications

Citrate-related hypocalcaemia/hypomagnesaemia, early hyperkalaemia/later shifts, hypothermia, dilution/consumption, acidosis then possible citrate-related alkalosis, TACO/TRALI, haemolysis, contamination and errors need active surveillance. Source control and restored perfusion treat shock acidosis; routine bicarbonate does not replace these. Avoid treating a normal initial Hb as reassuring. Special populations use weight-based volumes and dedicated protocols.

## Build, stand down and audit

Define activation/escalation, logistics, lab access, rapid infuser/salvage staffing, emergency stock, packs, communication, special populations and stop rules. Stand down clearly once bleeding is controlled, reconcile unused products and transition to individual replacement/prophylaxis. Audit timeliness, ratios/targets, wastage, complications and outcome; rehearse with simulation.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Transfer principles without treating obstetric and trauma bleeding as identical

A 2026 BJA narrative review distinguishes loss/dilution of factors from pathological fibrinogen destruction in acute obstetric coagulopathy. Pregnancy baseline haemostasis, the cause of bleeding and the coagulopathy phenotype differ from nonpregnant trauma. Consequently a trauma-derived pack ratio is not proof of optimal treatment for every PPH. Start urgent resuscitation/source control, then use the obstetric pathway, serial fibrinogen/VEM and clinical response to individualise haemostatic replacement. This is a transferable Set 2 haemostasis point; detailed obstetric emergency management remains in its primary set. [Primary author-repository abstract](https://orca.cardiff.ac.uk/id/eprint/187688/) reviewed; not a full-text review.

## Self-marking checklist
- Uses clinical early MHP activation
- Roles, communication and source control
- Explains ratios and adult platelet equivalence
- Transitions to monitored deficit-guided therapy
- TXA indication plus temperature/calcium/fibrinogen
- Recognises metabolic, immune and volume complications
- Emergency blood selection and special populations
- Stand-down, logistics, audit and simulation
- Explains why obstetric coagulopathy and trauma evidence cannot be treated as identical

items.title: 5. Jehovah's Witness for major abdominal surgery
items.q: A 55-year-old Jehovah's Witness with a haemoglobin of 105 g/L is scheduled for an elective major abdominal operation. Discuss your perioperative management.
items.a:
## Consent and a feasible treatment plan

Discuss privately with the patient, check capacity/voluntariness and document **each accepted or declined intervention**: donor RBC/plasma/platelets, cryoprecipitate, fractions/concentrates, albumin, cell salvage, continuous circuit, swab washing and ANH. Do not infer choices from religion or ask relatives to overrule a capable adult. Explain expected blood loss, residual risk including death, alternatives, advance decisions and emergency limits. Involve senior surgery/anaesthesia, haematology/PBM and a liaison service if the patient wants. If an elective operation cannot be offered within those limits, arrange an alternative team/approach with continuity of care; do not abandon care.

## Optimise before elective major surgery

Hb 105 g/L warrants cause-based investigation: FBC/indices, reticulocytes, ferritin/TSAT with CRP, renal function, B12/folate when indicated and investigation of losses. Correct genuine deficiencies, use IV iron if the interval/absorption favours it, and consider ESA only with specialist advice, thrombosis assessment and acceptability of the preparation. Recheck response and discuss deferral/less invasive surgery; do not aim “as high as possible” with an ESA. Review antithrombotics and bleeding disorders, minimise sampling and agree the surgical rescue plan.

## Theatre and postoperative conservation

Experienced surgery, meticulous haemostasis, appropriate TXA, accepted salvage/selected ANH, normothermia, physiological calcium/pH and targeted haemostatic agents if accepted. Deliberate hypotension is not safe simply because donor blood is refused—maintain coronary/cerebral/renal perfusion. Maximise oxygenation and flow and reduce avoidable demand (pain, fever, shivering); **do not deliberately cool the patient**, which worsens coagulopathy. rFVIIa and haemoglobin-based oxygen carriers are not routine substitutes; exceptional rescue needs specialist/regulatory access and individual consent.

Include senior theatre briefing, ready access to the documented choices and a plan for deterioration. Explicitly discuss acceptability of RRT, plasma exchange or ECMO if relevant; acceptance of salvage does not imply acceptance of every circuit. If wishes are unclear during incapacity, urgently involve senior clinical/medicolegal support under the local jurisdiction. A conscious patient may change a decision, but reassess capacity, pain/distress and possible coercion rather than pressuring them mid-crisis. Arrange staff support after a serious adverse outcome.

Plan monitored recovery/ICU according to risk, detect ongoing loss early, minimise phlebotomy, treat deficiency and continue a documented anaemia/thrombosis strategy. Record the accepted emergency ceiling clearly for every team.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Individual capacity/consent and exact product choices
- Documents emergency limits and coordinates an appropriate team
- Investigates Hb 105 and treats the cause before elective surgery
- Uses selective iron/ESA with reassessment
- Appropriate TXA/salvage/ANH only if accepted
- Maintains perfusion and normothermia, avoids unproven routine rescue
- Postoperative monitoring, sampling conservation and handover

items.title: 6. Sickle cell disease for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease (HbSS) requires an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Discuss his perioperative management.
items.a:
## Risk and multidisciplinary planning

HbSS produces deoxygenation-related HbS polymerisation, haemolysis and vaso-occlusion. Assess crises, acute chest syndrome/stroke, baseline Hb/SpO₂, pulmonary hypertension, renal/cardiac disease, infection/asplenia, analgesic use and prior transfusion reactions/alloantibodies. Involve a sickle specialist and blood bank early; provide appropriately phenotype/genotype-matched RBCs if needed.

## Transfusion before this operation

ASH conditionally favours preoperative transfusion for GA lasting >1 h, but the decision depends on genotype, baseline Hb, surgical risk, phenotype and previous transfusion harms. For Hb <90 g/L, simple transfusion may achieve an appropriate **90–110 g/L** range; avoid excessive viscosity, commonly not exceeding **110 g/L** with simple transfusion. If baseline Hb is already >90–100, exchange may be preferable when transfusion is beneficial; very high-risk surgery or severe phenotype can warrant a lower HbS target (often <30%). **HbS <30–40% is not mandatory for every laparoscopic cholecystectomy**, and Hb >100 is not universally prohibited. Do not delay emergency surgery merely to reach an elective target.

## Anaesthesia and recovery

Avoid prolonged fasting, hypoxaemia, hypovolaemia/overload, hypothermia, acidosis, hypotension and venous stasis. Use approved clear-fluid policy and IV fluid if needed rather than automatic deficit replacement. GA/laparoscopy and regional analgesia can be appropriate; manage insufflation/ventilation and monitor perfusion. Provide effective multimodal analgesia without hypoventilation, warming, antibiotics for the procedure and indicated asplenia/infection care.

Postoperative lung expansion/incentive spirometry, mobilisation, euvolaemia and suitable VTE prophylaxis are important. Suspect **acute chest syndrome** with a new infiltrate plus fever/respiratory features/hypoxaemia: urgent specialist review, oxygen/respiratory support, infection treatment, analgesia and simple/exchange transfusion as indicated. Distinguish PE, atelectasis and surgical complications from painful crisis. High-flow oxygen is not routine when saturation is normal.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains sickling, phenotype and organ risk
- Specialist and antigen-matched blood planning
- Individualises simple/exchange transfusion and avoids hyperviscosity
- Uses ASH targets without universal HbS or Hb100 rule
- Protects oxygenation, temperature, perfusion and hydration
- Analgesia, lung expansion, VTE prevention and mobilisation
- Recognises and treats acute chest syndrome

items.title: 7. TRALI versus TACO
items.q: Compare transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) and transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) in terms of pathophysiology, diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Similar presentation, different dominant mechanism

Both cause hypoxaemia and bilateral pulmonary opacities after transfusion; mixed cases occur. **TRALI is permeability oedema**, typically during/within 6 h, without hydrostatic overload as the main cause. Type I has no ARDS risk factor; Type II may occur with an ARDS risk factor or mild pre-existing ARDS if respiratory status was stable for the preceding 12 h. **TACO is hydrostatic overload**, during/within 12 h, and may follow a small volume in a susceptible patient.

| Finding | Supports TRALI | Supports TACO |
|---|---|---|
| Context | Inflammatory susceptibility; donor antibody/neutrophil/endothelial mechanisms | Cardiac/renal impairment, low body weight, rapid infusion or positive balance |
| BP/JVP | Hypotension or normal BP can occur | Hypertension/JVP rise common, but neither obligatory |
| Echo/volume assessment | Overload is not dominant; cardiac disease may coexist | Evidence of raised filling pressure/congestion supports |
| BNP/NT-proBNP | Cannot exclude/confirm alone, especially in critical illness | Elevated or increased value is supportive, not a stand-alone diagnosis |
| Response | Diuretics do not treat pure permeability injury | Diuresis/afterload/respiratory support often helps |

There is no reliable bedside “low BNP = TRALI, high BNP = TACO” rule. Do not assume normal EF excludes TACO or abnormal EF excludes TRALI. Consider aspiration, anaphylaxis, bacterial sepsis, AHTR, cardiogenic/negative-pressure oedema and evolving ARDS.

## Immediate management

Stop transfusion, assess ABC, give oxygen/ventilatory support, check identifiers and alert blood bank. Preserve the bag/set; maintain access through a fresh line/set without flushing the implicated unit. Send reaction/haemolysis/sepsis tests as indicated; obtain CXR/lung ultrasound, echo, gas and volume assessment without delaying support.

TRALI: supportive lung-protective ventilation if needed, cautious haemodynamic treatment and specialist/ICU care; no routine steroids or diuresis unless a coexisting indication exists. Report so the blood service can investigate and manage co-components. TACO: stop unnecessary fluids, sit up if appropriate, oxygen/CPAP and diuretics, treat heart/renal failure. Reassess uncertainty as treatment proceeds.

## Prevention

Avoid unnecessary transfusion. TACO risk assessment, single-unit prescribing/reassessment for stable patients, slower or divided transfusions and selective diuretic use. TRALI mitigation relies on donor/plasma policies and reporting; bedside screening cannot prevent all cases.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Mechanism and 6 h versus 12 h windows
- TRALI I/II and coexistence with cardiac disease
- Uses BNP/echo as supportive, not definitive
- Stops transfusion, fresh access, identity/blood-bank steps
- Differential and targeted investigations
- Ventilatory support and indication-specific diuretics
- Prevention and haemovigilance

items.title: 8. Disseminated intravascular coagulation
items.q: Discuss the diagnosis and management of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) in the perioperative period.
items.a:
## Identify the syndrome and cause

DIC is acquired systemic coagulation activation, microvascular thrombosis, consumption and dysregulated fibrinolysis. Phenotype varies: septic DIC often suppresses fibrinolysis; obstetric catastrophe/APL may cause severe hyperfibrinolytic bleeding. Triggers include sepsis, severe tissue injury, obstetric events, malignancy/APL and acute haemolytic reactions. Massive transfusion can produce dilutional coagulopathy and is not synonymous with DIC.

Look for diffuse oozing, purpura, limb/circuit thrombosis and renal/neurological/respiratory injury. Trend platelets, PT/APTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer/FDP, blood film and haemolysis studies. **Normal/high fibrinogen early in sepsis does not exclude DIC**. ISTH overt score uses platelets, fibrin markers, PT prolongation and fibrinogen; ≥5 supports overt DIC only with an appropriate disorder and serial assessment. APTT and VEM may be normal early; neither rules it out.

## Exclude time-critical mimics

TTP/HUS: MAHA/schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, organ injury and often relatively normal PT/APTT; urgent haematology, ADAMTS13 sample and treatment without waiting if TTP likely. HIT: timed platelet fall with thrombosis after heparin; stop heparin and use an alternative anticoagulant. Also assess liver disease, drugs, marrow failure, vitamin K deficiency and simple dilution.

## Treat the driver and phenotype

Source control/antibiotics, obstetric control/delivery as appropriate, immediate specialist ATRA for suspected APL, or other cause treatment; organ support in parallel. For active bleeding/urgent procedures, replace the demonstrated deficit: platelets often to >50 ×10⁹/L (higher for critical sites), fibrinogen commonly >1.5–2 g/L, plasma for significant multiple-factor deficiency; RBCs for delivery/haemorrhage. **PCC is not complete DIC replacement** and routine use can worsen thrombosis. Do not give FFP just to normalise an INR in a nonbleeding patient.

VTE prophylaxis when safe; treatment anticoagulation may be justified for a predominant thrombotic phenotype with specialist advice. TXA is generally avoided in thrombotic DIC, but a selected severe hyperfibrinolytic bleeding phenotype requires disease-specific specialist judgment. Avoid neuraxial puncture in active DIC and minimise unnecessary invasive procedures. Repeat clinical/laboratory assessment because treatment needs change.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Systemic coagulation plus variable fibrinolysis
- Identifies cause and serial diagnostic pattern
- Normal fibrinogen/APTT does not exclude early disease
- Uses ISTH score in the right context
- Differentiates TTP, HIT, liver disease and dilution
- Cause treatment plus deficit replacement only when indicated
- Qualifies PCC, TXA and heparin; procedure precautions

items.title: 9. ITP before laparoscopic splenectomy
items.q: A 45-year-old woman with a platelet count of 35 x 10^9/L due to immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) requires an elective laparoscopic splenectomy. Discuss your perioperative management.
items.a:
## Assess the patient rather than the count alone

Confirm ITP/true thrombocytopenia, trend and bleeding phenotype, medications, other cell lines/film, previous treatment response and competing DIC/TMA/HIT/liver disease. At **35 ×10⁹/L**, elective splenectomy needs a haematology/surgical haemostatic plan; GA is generally preferable to neuraxial techniques at this count. A single 70–80 threshold is not universally safe for neuraxial anaesthesia.

## Improve haemostasis before elective surgery

Haematology may use corticosteroids, IVIG (commonly 1 g/kg with response/repeat guided by protocol), or a TPO-receptor agonist when time permits. Account for adverse effects, thrombosis and steroid adrenal suppression. Selected anti-D treatment is not routine and has haemolysis risks. Major surgery often uses ≥50 ×10⁹/L as a general component threshold, but **ITP-specific elective major-surgery targets may be higher**, depending on procedure and team guidance. Splenectomy may be feasible at lower counts in experienced centres; avoid imposing one universal target.

Platelets have a short survival in ITP. Do not transfuse prophylactically simply to normalise a number, but **life-threatening bleeding or an urgent invasive operation can justify platelet transfusion alongside IVIG/steroids**. During splenectomy, timing near/after splenic artery control may improve survival **if the patient is stable**; never delay lifesaving platelets until clamping as an absolute rule.

## Anaesthesia and postoperative plan

Gentle airway/vascular instrumentation, avoid unnecessary nasal/IM trauma and NSAIDs, source control and appropriate haemostatic adjuncts. Assess accepted block alternatives by site/compressibility. Plan blood/platelet availability, sufficient IV access and response monitoring. Consider steroid cover by actual exposure.

Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Hib, asplenia antibiotic/fever education and local prophylaxis plan. After splenectomy monitor count, bleeding, infection and portal/systemic thrombosis; provide appropriate mechanical/pharmacological VTE prevention when haemostasis permits. A postoperative platelet rise does not justify ignoring thrombosis risk.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## IVIg is a product with important hazards

IVIg provides pooled IgG with immunomodulatory effects, including altered Fc-mediated immune-cell activation; it can produce a relatively rapid, often temporary platelet response in ITP. Confirm indication, product, total grams, dosing weight and monitoring with haematology. Use the current product-specific infusion chart: a concentration and a rate in mL/kg/hour must not be confused with a dose in g/kg. Watch for infusion reactions/anaphylaxis, thrombosis, renal injury, aseptic meningitis and haemolysis/positive DAT. Assess fluid tolerance and renal/thrombotic risk; select an appropriate formulation and rate. It is not a risk-free substitute for donor platelets and does not make every urgent procedure safe immediately. [IVIG24](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534923001427) [IVIGNZ](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/healthcare-professionals/transfusion-medicine/transfusion-medicine-handbook/5-fractionated-products/5-4-9-privigen-nz-privigen-normal-immunoglobulin-10-intravenous-immunoglobulin-ivig)

## Self-marking checklist
- Confirms diagnosis, trend and bleeding risk
- Specialist elective target rather than generic count rule
- Steroid/IVIG/TPO options and time to response
- Platelets for severe bleeding/urgent intervention, not clamp-only rule
- Appropriate GA and instrumentation precautions
- Asplenia vaccination/infection planning
- Postoperative VTE, count and bleeding surveillance
- Explains IVIg mechanism/temporary benefit and renal, thrombotic, haemolytic and infusion risks

items.title: 10. Tranexamic acid: pharmacology, evidence and risks
items.q: Discuss the pharmacology, evidence and risks of tranexamic acid in the perioperative period.
items.a:
## Pharmacology and indication-specific dosing

TXA is a synthetic lysine analogue that reduces plasminogen binding to fibrin and inhibits fibrinolysis. It does not replace factors or stop an unsecured vessel. Predominantly renally cleared (half-life roughly 2–3 h): use indication/product-specific dose adjustment. Trauma commonly **1 g IV over 10 min then 1 g over 8 h within 3 h of injury**; PPH **1 g over 10 min within 3 h of birth**, repeat once after 30 min if continuing or within 24 h if recurrent. Elective orthopaedic regimens vary (IV/oral/topical); do not transfer one infusion schedule to all surgery.

## Evaluate the evidence

- CRASH-2: early bleeding-trauma benefit; late administration after 3 h can increase bleeding death. Do not wait for VEM-confirmed lysis.
- WOMAN: reduced death from bleeding in PPH, particularly early; not proof that prophylactic TXA benefits every delivery.
- ATACAS: less bleeding/transfusion in cardiac surgery, with a seizure concern; dose and renal function matter.
- Orthopaedic evidence supports reduced blood loss/transfusion. **POISE-3** reduced its composite bleeding endpoint in major noncardiac surgery, but **cardiovascular noninferiority was not established**. Similar point estimates are not proof of safety equivalence.
- **TRACTION (2026)**: a hospital-policy cluster-crossover trial reduced RBC transfusion (7.4% vs 9.8%) and met its specified **VTE** noninferiority margin. This strengthens evidence in its mainly oncological major-surgery population; it does not retroactively change POISE-3's different composite safety result or prove zero thrombosis risk.
- HALT-IT: no bleeding-death benefit in GI bleeding and increased VTE/seizures; not routine treatment. CRASH-3's early TBI signal must be described by severity, not as universal neurological benefit.

## Harms and safe use

Dose-related seizures (cardiac/high-dose/renal accumulation), hypotension with rapid injection, selected thrombotic risk, visual adverse effects and urinary-tract clot obstruction are important. Avoid indiscriminate treatment of active thrombosis/thrombotic DIC; consider specialist phenotype-specific exceptions. Never give intrathecally: separate TXA from spinal local-anaesthetic storage, label syringes, verify route. Use renal-adjusted protocols and continue appropriate postoperative thromboprophylaxis. Balance trial-specific benefit against patient bleeding/thrombotic risk; TXA complements haemostasis.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Mechanism, renal clearance and dosing by indication
- Trauma/PPH early time windows
- Distinguishes efficacy from safety/noninferiority
- Correct POISE-3 and 2026 TRACTION interpretation
- GI/TBI evidence kept population-specific
- Seizures, renal/urinary/thrombotic risks
- Wrong-route prevention and haemostasis/prophylaxis

items.title: 11. FFP, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate and PCC
items.q: Compare fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate and prothrombin complex concentrate in the management of perioperative bleeding.
items.a:
## Treat the specific deficit

| Component | Contents / purpose | Typical approach | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| FFP | Multiple soluble clotting factors, including V/VIII, some fibrinogen | Often 10–15 mL/kg for significant factor deficit with bleeding/procedure, then assess | Volume, thawing, TACO/TRALI; not routine volume expansion or correction of mild INR alone |
| Cryoprecipitate | Concentrated fibrinogen with VIII, XIII, vWF/fibronectin | **NZ high-fibrinogen apheresis cryo: ≈1 unit/30 kg** is a local starting guide; NZBS estimates ≈1 g/L increment, with measured reassessment | Unit content differs markedly between countries; do not prescribe a universal “10-unit pool” |
| Fibrinogen concentrate | Standardised fibrinogen, small volume | Common adult initial 3–4 g under a critical-bleeding algorithm, adjusted to weight/deficit and response | Cost, thrombosis, reconstitution; acquired use subject to local approval, no platelet/other-factor replacement |
| 4F-PCC | II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S; product-specific heparin | Rapid VKA reversal with vitamin K; selected off-label Xa bleeding protocols | No fibrinogen/V/VIII replacement; thrombosis, HIT caution if heparin-containing; not routine trauma/DIC replacement |

NZ uses **Beriplex 4F-PCC** following the 2025 transition; historical Prothrombinex-VF dosing/composition should not be assumed interchangeable. Consult the current protocol and maximum/rate limits.

## Bedside selection and evidence

In ongoing major bleeding, source control and the MHP run concurrently with serial labs/VEM, temperature, iCa/pH and perfusion.
