Replace low fibrinogen early (commonly >1.5–2 g/L; obstetric ≥2), but do not give it before every other component regardless of the actual deficit. Low whole-clot strength with adequate fibrin contribution suggests a platelet problem; prolonged CT may reflect drug, fibrinogen or factor deficiency, not an automatic indication for PCC.

**FARES-II (2025)** supports PCC rather than plasma for selected post-CPB factor-replacement bleeding, with greater haemostatic effectiveness in its trial setting; it does not support empirical PCC for every trauma patient. See R32 for the worked evidence comparison.

**FIBRES** established **fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate** for 24-h component use in bleeding, hypofibrinogenaemic post-CPB adults—not the reverse trial claim, universal superiority, or guaranteed mortality benefit. PROCOAG discourages empirical 4F-PCC in all trauma bleeding. Repeat the clinical and measured response; a good laboratory number does not control a surgical vessel.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Obstetric haemostatic replacement is targeted therapy

Pregnancy has a higher baseline fibrinogen; a low-normal nonpregnant result can be important during PPH. In ongoing obstetric bleeding, use the local pathway, serial fibrinogen and validated VEM thresholds to identify a deficit; commonly aim at least 2 g/L. FIB-PPH, OBS2 and FIDEL did not justify routine empirical fibrinogen concentrate in women whose fibrinogen was already adequate. This does not show that correction of a true severe deficit is futile. Plasma is not a concentrated fibrinogen replacement, and a trauma ratio is not automatically optimal for every atonic PPH. Do not turn this into withholding emergency components during life-threatening uncontrolled bleeding while waiting for tests. Routine PCC is not established treatment of PPH; specialist rescue rFVIIa does not replace source control and carries thrombotic risk. Foreign cryoprecipitate unit content, costs and licensing must not be copied into NZ prescriptions. [OBHAEM24](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924000891)

## Self-marking checklist
- Correct contents and missing factors
- FFP indication, dose and volume burden
- NZ-specific cryo unit equivalence and measured response
- Fibrinogen concentrate indication/local approval
- 4F-PCC plus vitamin K, product and thrombosis/HIT caveats
- Correct FIBRES direction and trial population
- Uses deficit-directed selection alongside haemostasis
- Distinguishes targeted obstetric fibrinogen replacement from empirical concentrate use and universal trauma-pack extrapolation

items.title: 12. Drug-eluting stent on dual antiplatelets for hernia repair
items.q: A 65-year-old man had a drug-eluting coronary stent inserted 4 months ago and is taking aspirin and clopidogrel. He requires an elective hernia repair. Discuss your perioperative management.
items.a:
## Determine PCI indication and the risks of delay

Clarify whether the DES followed **ACS or chronic coronary disease**, complexity, prior stent thrombosis, cardiac function, current symptoms and adherence. Elective hernia repair can usually wait: ACC/AHA 2024 generally recommends delaying elective surgery requiring antiplatelet interruption for **≥6 months after DES for chronic disease, ≥12 months after ACS** (also consider complex PCI). Time-sensitive surgery may be considered from ≥3 months when delaying is worse; some other guidance allows earlier selected cases. Four months is not an automatic clearance or universal prohibition.

## Agree the antiplatelet plan

Senior anaesthesia, surgeon and interventional cardiologist should balance surgical bleeding, harm from delay and stent thrombosis. Continue aspirin perioperatively if feasible; it is not an unconditional instruction in catastrophic bleeding-risk surgery. For this usually low/moderate-bleeding-risk operation, continuation of DAPT may be feasible or postponement may be preferred. If interruption is agreed, clopidogrel is commonly stopped **5 days for surgery**, whereas ASRA neuraxial advice is **5–7 days**. Restart promptly once haemostasis permits with cardiology agreement; 24 h is a possible plan, not a universal fixed rule.

LMWH does **not** substitute for antiplatelet protection against stent thrombosis. IV cangrelor bridging is exceptional, specialist-led and resource-dependent, not a standard switch for every patient at 4 months. Platelets are not routine prophylactic “reversal”: ticagrelor's circulating drug inhibits transfused platelets; clopidogrel/prasugrel have different active-metabolite kinetics. DDAVP/TXA are not automatic treatments merely because a stent is present.

## Anaesthesia and recovery

Local/suitable superficial regional or GA can be appropriate. Deep plexus/neuraxial techniques require guideline-concordant interruption and catheter/restart planning; a generic “peripheral block” is not automatically safe. Maintain myocardial perfusion, avoid tachycardia, hypoxia, sustained hypotension and significant anaemia. Plan postoperative antiplatelet resumption, ECG/troponin surveillance when indicated, and rapid access to PCI if ischaemia occurs. Provide a written plan to the patient and all teams.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Clarifies ACS versus chronic disease and PCI complexity
- Uses 6/12-month elective and conditional time-sensitive framework
- Balances delay, stent thrombosis and procedure-specific bleeding
- Aspirin and P2Y12 plan with prompt restart
- Distinguishes surgery from neuraxial intervals
- No routine heparin substitute or cangrelor bridge
- Appropriate technique, perfusion and rescue pathway

items.title: 13. Neuraxial anaesthesia with antithrombotic therapy
items.q: Outline the guidelines for performing neuraxial anaesthesia in patients receiving antithrombotic therapy, including the management of suspected epidural haematoma.
items.a:
## Define the planned block and the drug exposure

Use the **ASRA fifth edition (2025)** and the current institutional protocol for neuraxial and deep plexus/deep peripheral blocks. Record the exact agent, low/high dose, indication, last dose, CrCl, interacting agents, platelet trend and bleeding phenotype. Catheter removal is itself an intervention. Routine surgical interruption, diagnostic lumbar puncture and neuraxial anaesthesia use different rules. There is **no universal safe platelet count** for every epidural/spinal; do not generalise obstetric consensus or a diagnostic-LP threshold.

## Representative minimum intervals

| Agent/regimen | Before needle placement | Postoperative dose / catheter constraints |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | Usually stop 5 days and **normalise INR** | Removal generally INR <1.5; INR surveillance and neurological observations if warfarin restarted with a catheter |
| IV UFH | Stop 4–6 h, normal coagulation assessment | Delay IV heparin ≥1 h after placement; avoid maintaining a catheter during continuous IV heparin; specialist plan if unanticipated anticoagulation |
| Low-dose SC UFH 5000 U twice/three times daily | 4–6 h or normal coagulation assessment | Remove 4–6 h after dose; ASRA permits immediate subsequent low-dose SC UFH. Higher SC doses require longer interruption |
| Once-daily low-dose LMWH | ≥12 h | First dose ≥12 h after placement; second ≥24 h after first. Remove ≥12 h after last dose; next dose ≥4 h after removal |
| Twice-daily low-dose LMWH | ≥12 h | First dose following day and ≥12 h after placement; **remove catheter before commencing**, then wait ≥4 h |
| High-dose LMWH | ≥24 h; renal impairment/age may require longer or residual assay assessment | Resume ≥24 h after lower-risk or 48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery; remove catheter ≥4 h before first dose, which must also be ≥24 h after placement |
| Aspirin/NSAID alone | No specific ASRA neuraxial interruption | Combinations, additional coagulopathy and pain-procedure guidance change risk |
| Clopidogrel / prasugrel / ticagrelor | 5–7 d / 7–10 d / 5 d | Maintenance dose can generally restart immediately after removal; wait ≥6 h for a loading dose. Avoid indwelling catheters with prasugrel/ticagrelor; clopidogrel has narrow guideline exceptions |
| High-dose apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban | ≥72 h | Placement/removal ≥24 h before first high dose, plus surgical haemostasis requirements |
| Low-dose apixaban | ≥36 h | Placement/removal ≥6 h before first low dose |
| Low-dose rivaroxaban | ≥24 h (30 h if CrCl <30) | Placement/removal ≥6 h before first low dose |
| High-dose dabigatran | ≥72 h if CrCl ≥50; ≥120 h if CrCl 30–49 | Placement/removal ≥24 h before first high dose |
| Low-dose dabigatran | ≥48 h | Placement/removal ≥6 h before first low dose |

For dabigatran and CrCl <30, avoid neuraxial/deep blocks unless a validated drug level is <30 ng/mL. ASRA permits selected residual drug-level approaches (DOAC <30 ng/mL; Xa activity ≤0.1 IU/mL for appropriate Xa assays), but assay interpretation and suitability are specialist decisions, not an invitation to shorten intervals routinely. Fondaparinux is dose/renal-function-specific; consult its dedicated guidance. Avoid neuraxial techniques during active argatroban/bivalirudin treatment. Do not use reversal solely to enable an elective block.

## Technique, surveillance and suspected haematoma

Use an experienced operator, ultrasound when useful, minimise traumatic attempts and document the catheter/dose plan. Check platelets with heparin exposure >4 days; consider HIT. Delay LMWH initiation for 24 h after bloody/traumatic placement under the applicable guideline and discuss thrombosis protection. Use dilute epidural local anaesthetic and an explicit motor/sensory surveillance plan. New weakness, sensory change, severe back pain or sphincter dysfunction requires **immediate assessment, stop the infusion, urgent MRI and neurosurgical consultation in parallel**. Reverse coagulopathy appropriately; decompress as soon as indicated, ideally within hours—do not wait for an 8–12-hour deadline. Continue surveillance after removal.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Peripartum application: dose, unplanned labour and postpartum restart

Establish whether LMWH is prophylaxis after previous VTE or treatment of acute VTE/mechanical-valve thrombosis risk. **Highlow** did not demonstrate superior prevention of recurrent VTE with intermediate versus low-dose LMWH in its previous-VTE pregnancy population; higher dosing also reduced access to neuraxial techniques after unplanned labour. Do not extrapolate this to underdosing an acute PE or mechanical valve.

Provide a written antenatal plan for contractions/ruptured membranes, planned delivery, last dose, alternative analgesia/anaesthesia and postpartum restart. For intermediate-dose LMWH there is insufficient evidence for one precise 12–24-hour neuraxial interval; identify the actual dose and seek a conservative specialist/local plan. Recent therapeutic LMWH, renal impairment and combinations cannot be cleared by a normal APTT or routine VEM. Switching to UFH near delivery is selected for specific risk/logistical reasons, not mandatory for every woman receiving prophylaxis.

Postpartum restart requires adequate obstetric/surgical haemostasis **and** the applicable placement/removal-to-next-dose intervals. A minimum interval after delivery alone is not permission to give treatment-dose LMWH with an unsafe epidural catheter. The 2025 review cites older ASRA guidance; the fifth-edition dose-specific and catheter rules in the table above take precedence where updated. Mechanical-valve management also requires the separate Pregnancy Heart Team plan in 2023.1 Q6. [PERIP25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924001094)

## Self-marking checklist
- Identifies agent/dose/time, CrCl, block depth and catheter
- Distinguishes surgical hold from neuraxial rules
- Correct low/high-dose LMWH placement and restart constraints
- Distinguishes once-daily from twice-daily catheter practice
- Updated dose-specific DOAC intervals and restart
- Antiplatelet/UFH rules and additional bleeding risks
- No universal platelet threshold or routine elective reversal
- Immediate deficit assessment/MRI/neurosurgery; no waiting for a deadline
- Applies antenatal/unplanned-labour and postpartum planning without equating prophylaxis with acute-VTE/valve treatment
- Recognises intermediate-dose uncertainty and prioritises current dose-specific catheter guidance

items.title: 14. Interpreting a ROTEM or TEG trace
items.q: Describe how you would interpret a ROTEM or TEG trace in a bleeding patient and how it would alter your management.
items.a:
## Interpret in the context of active bleeding

First confirm patient/sample, platform/cartridge, time after activation, temperature, drug exposure and the surgical source. Standard ROTEM/TEG are low-shear whole-blood assays, not complete endothelial/platelet-function tests. Classical cup/pin devices and newer TEG resonance platforms differ. EXTEM is tissue-factor activated; INTEM contact activated; HEPTEM adds heparinase; FIBTEM inhibits platelet contribution; APTEM uses an antifibrinolytic reagent (check the local cartridge). TEG R/K/angle/MA and ROTEM CT/CFT/A5/MCF are analogous but not numerically interchangeable.

| Pattern | Interpretation and next step |
|---|---|
| Long CT/R | Drug/heparin, factor or severe fibrinogen deficit. Compare paired heparinase tests and labs; reverse a demonstrated drug effect or replace indicated factors, not automatic PCC |
| Low whole-clot strength plus low FIBTEM/functional fibrin | Low fibrinogen/function → cryo or concentrate in a validated algorithm |
| Low whole-clot strength with adequate fibrin contribution | Low platelet count/contribution → count/function assessment and indicated platelets; standard VEM cannot identify every antiplatelet defect |
| Progressive narrowing | Lysis: **TEG LY30 and ROTEM ML increase; ROTEM LI30 (remaining firmness) decreases**. Confirm assay/timing; consider APTEM comparison and appropriate antifibrinolysis |
| Apparently normal trace with continued bleeding | Search surgical source AND defects not measured (vWD, platelet dysfunction, some DOACs/FXIII defects), temperature and sampling errors |

## Act and reassess

Use the validated local assay/setting-specific thresholds, not a universal FIBTEM/LY30 cutoff across cardiac, obstetric and trauma care. Correct temperature/iCa/perfusion and give the treatment for the identified deficit. Repeat a clinically useful early trace after treatment and track actual bleeding. **Normal VEM does not exclude DOAC activity or rule out mild/moderate fibrinolysis**, and should not withhold indicated early TXA in major trauma.

## Evaluate limitations and implementation

Most instruments measure at 37°C, potentially masking hypothermic dysfunction. Endothelium, vWF/platelet-drug effects and protein-C pathways are incompletely represented; reagent, haematocrit, timing, handling and operator/QC matter. VEM-guided algorithms can reduce components, particularly in cardiac/liver settings; mortality estimates vary and the large ITACTIC primary trauma result was neutral. The Blue Book 2025 emphasises contextual algorithms, fibrinogen-first correction **when deficient**, training, result access and audit; it does not make every published threshold a universal prescription.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Defines correct platform, assays and context
- Interprets initiation, fibrin and platelet contribution separately
- Correct LY30/ML versus LI30 direction
- Drug/heparin comparison without automatic PCC
- Normal trace does not exclude every bleeding disorder
- Local validated thresholds and repeat assessment
- Does not delay clinically indicated trauma TXA
- Limitations, evidence and implementation

items.title: 15. Beta-thalassaemia major for splenectomy
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic considerations for a patient with beta-thalassaemia major presenting for a splenectomy.
items.a:
## Multisystem disease and operation-specific risks

Transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia causes ineffective erythropoiesis/haemolysis, marrow expansion and iron loading. Review regular transfusions/chelation, baseline Hb, alloantibodies, reactions and infection history. Splenomegaly and hypersplenism may cause cytopenias; splenectomy adds haemorrhage, infection and portal/systemic thrombosis risk.

Preoperatively involve haematology and assess ECG/echo, cardiac MRI T2* where available, heart failure/arrhythmia/pulmonary hypertension; hepatic fibrosis/function; diabetes, thyroid/parathyroid dysfunction/calcium; renal function, osteoporosis and growth/skeletal change. Blood-bank planning requires compatible antigen-matched blood with historical antibodies respected. Routine chronic targets are often around **95–105 g/L pretransfusion**, but perioperative targets depend on cardiac disease and the specialist regimen; do not apply a generic ICU 70 threshold.

## Anaesthetic plan

Maxillary expansion, dentition and skeletal abnormalities may complicate mask/intubation; prepare a tailored airway plan rather than assuming every patient is difficult. Protect fragile bones and pressure areas. Maintain oxygenation, temperature, perfusion/rhythm and carefully judged volume in iron-overload cardiomyopathy. Use invasive monitoring for the actual cardiac/bleeding risk, not automatically in all cases. Assess platelet/coagulation status and anatomy before regional techniques.

RBCs should be leukodepleted/appropriately matched; **thalassaemia alone does not automatically require irradiated RBCs**. NZ platelet irradiation follows blood-service policy. Salvage in haemoglobinopathy is a specialist decision, not an unqualified routine option.

## Splenectomy and recovery

Plan vaccines, local antibiotic prophylaxis and fever/asplenia education; time vaccination before elective splenectomy where feasible. Anticipate splenic-bed bleeding, postoperative thrombocytosis and portal-vein thrombosis. Provide appropriate VTE prevention, postoperative cardiac/respiratory monitoring, analgesia, glucose/electrolyte review and a coordinated transfusion/chelation plan. Trait/minor disease has very different risk from transfusion-dependent major disease; do not prescribe iron for microcytosis unless deficiency is demonstrated.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains major disease and splenectomy risks
- Cardiac iron, hepatic/endocrine/renal and skeletal assessment
- Airway, bone/positioning and monitoring plan
- Antibody-compatible blood and specialist Hb target
- Does not mandate irradiation/salvage for every case
- Vaccination, antibiotics and asplenia education
- Bleeding, VTE/portal thrombosis and chronic-care follow-up

items.title: 16. ANH, autologous donation and cell salvage
items.q: Discuss the role of acute normovolaemic haemodilution (ANH), preoperative autologous donation and cell salvage in reducing allogeneic transfusion.
items.a:
## Compare the interventions by what they return

| Technique | Method and useful setting | Benefit and limitations |
|---|---|---|
| ANH | Collect a **patient-specific volume** of autologous whole blood after induction, maintain normovolaemia, label/store and return under protocol | Fewer RBCs lost per mL shed; returns platelets/factors as well as RBCs. Requires adequate baseline Hb/reserve and predictable loss; avoid arbitrary 1–2-L removal or a universal Hb80 nadir |
| Predeposit donation | Store the patient's donated units before a planned operation | May help rare antibodies/limited matched supply, but causes preoperative anaemia, wastage, logistics/clerical and bacterial risks; rarely routine under modern PBM |
| Washed intraoperative salvage | Collect, centrifuge, wash and return RBCs | Reduces donor exposure with sufficient recoverable loss; trained staff, cost, contamination and haemolysis risks; essentially no haemostatic-factor/platelet replacement |
| Postoperative drain systems | Device-specific recovery with or without washing | Unwashed products can contain free Hb/cytokines/activated debris; evidence and local approval differ; not interchangeable with washed intraoperative salvage |

## Evaluate contemporary evidence

Cell salvage can reduce donor exposure in selected operations; volume and case mix determine cost-effectiveness, and donor-exposure reduction is not automatically survival benefit. Older small ANH trials/meta-analyses suggested benefit in some settings, but the **2025 multinational RCT (2010 CPB patients)** did not reduce the proportion receiving donor RBCs (27.3% vs 29.2%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.81–1.07). This argues against claiming routine ANH benefit in all cardiac surgery while not resolving every selected noncardiac scenario. Predeposit can reduce allogeneic exposure yet increase total transfusion/anaemia and waste; assess the net outcome.

## Implement within PBM

Treat anaemia and review drugs first; use surgical haemostasis, appropriate TXA, normothermia, physiological calcium/pH and rational component decisions. Define staff competence, exact collection/storage/return limits, labels, contamination handling, emergency fallback and audit. Patient acceptance is individual: continuous circuit, disconnected storage and swab washing may have different consent decisions. Do not promise these techniques avoid all need for donor products during catastrophic bleeding.

## Other proposed conservation techniques

Hypervolaemic haemodilution lacks robust evidence for safety/clinical benefit and risks dilution/overload; it is not a routine replacement for ANH. Local haemostatic agents and tourniquets can improve the field in suitable operations, but reduced visible loss or faster local haemostasis is not automatically reduced total blood loss, transfusion or better outcomes. Evaluate patient-specific vascular, thrombotic and organ risks. The 2026 blood-refusal review's older ANH meta-analytic benefit estimates do not override the newer large neutral CPB trial.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains ANH physiology and patient-specific volume/reserve
- Returns whole blood versus washed RBC distinction
- Predeposit anaemia/waste and limited indications
- Salvage and unwashed drain-product differences
- Includes neutral 2025 ANH trial without overgeneralising
- Combines with PBM and appropriate selection
- Consent, traceability, storage and fallback/audit

items.title: 17. Risks of allogeneic transfusion and how to minimise them
items.q: Discuss the risks of allogeneic blood transfusion and how they can be minimised.
items.a:
## Immediate and delayed risks

Immediate: incompatible/wrong-patient haemolysis, bacterial contamination (particularly platelets), anaphylaxis/allergy, FNHTR, TRALI, **TACO**, hypotensive reactions and metabolic complications during rapid large-volume exposure. Delayed: alloimmunisation/delayed haemolysis, post-transfusion purpura, TA-GVHD, infection and chronic iron loading. Immunomodulation and associations with infection/cancer outcomes require causal caution: sicker, bleeding patients are more likely to receive blood. Do not teach that transfusion has proven to cause every observational adverse outcome.

Wrong-blood errors are catastrophic and preventable, but **TACO is a major cause of transfusion morbidity/death**; no single statement that clerical error is always the “biggest risk” is accurate across denominators. Modern donor selection/testing make viral transmission very rare; use current NZ haemovigilance estimates if quoting numbers. “HIV, HBV and HCV all <1 per million” is not a verified universal/local figure. Residual bacterial/emerging-pathogen risks vary by product and place.

## Reduce exposure and choose the right component

PBM: investigate/treat anaemia, minimise surgical/phlebotomy loss, use appropriate TXA/salvage, and rational thresholds. In a stable nonbleeding adult give one RBC unit then reassess; active haemorrhage needs a different approach. Obtain informed consent about indication, alternatives and material risks.

ABO/Rh-compatible blood, historical antibody identification, antigen-negative products where needed and a validated bedside independent identification process prevent major errors. Leukodepletion reduces some febrile/CMV risks; **irradiation prevents TA-GVHD in specific at-risk recipients and is not equivalent to leukodepletion**. NZ platelets are irradiated routinely; RBC indications depend on diagnosis/treatment, transplant, HLA/family donation and blood-service advice. Selected washed/IgA-deficient products are used for appropriate severe allergy, not for every incidental IgA deficiency.

Assess TACO risk (age, low weight, heart/renal disease, severe anaemia), prescribe the rate/volume, monitor baseline and early observations and consider divided units/diuretic in selected patients. Maintain the cold chain, approved filter/warmer rules and traceability. Recognise reactions, stop the implicated unit promptly, investigate/report and arrange future-product precautions.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Immediate immune, septic, volume and metabolic risks
- Delayed alloimmune/TA-GVHD/iron/infection risks
- Qualifies causal immunomodulation and infection estimates
- PBM and stable single-unit practice
- Bedside identification and compatible/antigen-matched components
- Distinguishes leukodepletion, irradiation and washing
- TACO risk/rate/monitoring and reaction/reporting plan

items.title: 18. Bleeding in renal failure and cirrhosis
items.q: Discuss the causes of abnormal bleeding in a patient with chronic renal failure and a patient with cirrhosis, and how you would manage each perioperatively.
items.a:
## Uraemia: primarily a qualitative platelet problem

Uraemic toxins, impaired adhesion/aggregation, endothelial mediators, anaemia and dialysis anticoagulation contribute; count/PT/APTT can be normal. Assess bleeding history, antithrombotics, dialysis timing, Hb/count and intended procedure. Optimise dialysis with a plan for residual heparin, treat demonstrated anaemia under renal guidance and avoid NSAIDs. **DDAVP 0.3 micrograms/kg IV over 20–30 min** may transiently improve clinically important bleeding/procedural haemostasis: monitor sodium, restrict appropriate free water and anticipate tachyphylaxis. Do not transfuse to a universal Hb100 solely for platelet function. Platelets, cryo, oestrogen or renal-adjusted TXA are specialist-selected rescue/indication-specific options, not a routine combination for every CKD patient.

## Cirrhosis: fragile rebalanced haemostasis

Reduced procoagulants coexist with reduced anticoagulants (protein C/S/antithrombin), increased VWF/FVIII, thrombocytopenia and sometimes dysfibrinogenaemia. Portal pressure/vascular lesions can drive bleeding; renal failure/infection alter the balance. **INR is not a global bleeding-risk test**, but neither is VEM a complete validated predictor of every procedure's bleeding. Assess clinical bleeding, platelets/fibrinogen, drugs, renal function and procedure; VEM can help guide active bleeding/reduce unnecessary components.

Do not give prophylactic FFP to normalise INR. Treat source/portal-hypertensive bleeding by the appropriate endoscopic/medical pathway, vitamin K only if deficiency plausible, and use platelets/fibrinogen/plasma for a clinically relevant deficit in bleeding/high-risk intervention. Avoid unnecessary large-volume plasma, but **PCC is not a universally safer substitute**; it can provoke thrombosis and does not replace all deficits. TXA is **not routine for variceal/GI bleeding** (HALT-IT); a documented hyperfibrinolytic surgical phenotype is different. A low-CVP technique is operation-specific (e.g. selected liver resection), not a blanket prescription in shocked cirrhosis.

## Shared plan

Specialist input, source control, normothermia, physiological iCa/pH and careful fluid/perfusion management. Individualise regional anaesthesia by haemostasis/function/drugs, assess both bleeding and thrombosis, and reassess after each treatment.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Uraemic qualitative platelet mechanisms
- Dialysis, anaemia review and DDAVP safety
- Avoids a routine rescue-drug cocktail/Hb target
- Explains rebalanced cirrhotic haemostasis
- Limits of INR and VEM
- Targeted products without reflex FFP/PCC or routine GI TXA
- Source/portal treatment, perfusion and specialist/regional plan

items.title: 19. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: central line and emergency laparotomy
items.q: A 30-year-old woman with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia on chemotherapy requires a central line and an emergency laparotomy. Discuss the perioperative issues.
items.a:
## Parallel urgent assessment and source-directed treatment

Discuss the cause/urgency of laparotomy with surgery, haematology and ICU. Assess ABC/perfusion, fever/neutropenic sepsis, bleeding, mucositis, bowel obstruction/ileus and recent chemotherapy/steroids. Obtain CBC/differential/film, coagulation/fibrinogen, renal/liver function, electrolytes/urate/LDH, gas/lactate and cultures where appropriate without delaying treatment. Review cardiac symptoms/anthracycline exposure, renal injury, tumour lysis and airway/vascular mass effects if suggested by diagnosis/symptoms; not every ALL patient has bleomycin exposure or a mediastinal mass.

## Infection, cytopenias and products

Prompt broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for **suspected neutropenic sepsis/intra-abdominal infection**, plus procedure prophylaxis as indicated; neutropenia alone does not create an identical antibiotic regimen for every operation. Treat volume/perfusion carefully with cardiomyopathy risk. Prepare antigen-compatible leukodepleted RBCs and platelets for the actual indication. Confirm **irradiated RBC/CMV requirements by specific treatment/transplant history**, not the generic label of malignancy; NZ platelets are irradiated routinely. Consider platelet refractoriness/alloimmunisation.

A count below 50 ×10⁹/L commonly prompts platelets for major nonneuraxial surgery; **compressible-site ultrasound-guided CVC thresholds differ** (2025 AABB conditionally recommends transfusion below 10 in adults). Use site, operator, function, trend and urgency; do not apply a universal platelet100 neuraxial permission rule. Active coagulopathy/sepsis/thrombocytopenia often makes neuraxial techniques unsuitable.

## Anaesthesia and recovery

Experienced airway management with care of mucosa; aspiration strategy appropriate to bowel pathology. A symptomatic mediastinal mass requires a dedicated positioning/airway/cardiovascular rescue plan before induction. Ultrasound-guided access with aseptic technique; invasive monitoring by instability/organ risk. Avoid fluid overload in cardiomyopathy, maintain warmth/calcium and source haemostasis; TXA only if indicated. If bleomycin was actually used, titrate oxygen to need—never withhold necessary oxygen. Steroid cover by exposure/risk.

ICU/HDU as indicated; monitor bleeding, infection, TLS/electrolytes/AKI, respiratory/cardiac dysfunction, pain and resumption of prophylaxis/oncological care. Explain that urgent surgery and resuscitation proceed together rather than waiting to normalise every blood result.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Urgency/source and specialist coordination
- Infection, marrow failure and relevant drug toxicity
- TLS/organ and mass effects assessed selectively
- Product modifications by actual indication
- Distinguishes CVC/major surgery/neuraxial thresholds
- Appropriate airway/access/perfusion precautions
- Postoperative organ, infection, bleeding/VTE and treatment plan

items.title: 20. Patient blood management and transfusion thresholds
items.q: Discuss the principles of patient blood management in the perioperative period and the evidence for restrictive versus liberal transfusion thresholds.
items.a:
## Three PBM pillars across the pathway

**Optimise red-cell mass/haemostasis:** early Hb and cause-based anaemia investigation, iron/B12/folate treatment where indicated, selective ESA, bleeding-history/drug review, appropriate surgery timing and blood-bank planning. **Reduce loss:** expert surgical control, appropriate TXA, selected salvage/ANH, normothermia/physiological iCa, targeted components and reduced phlebotomy. **Optimise tolerance of anaemia:** oxygenation, cardiac output/perfusion, reduce unnecessary demand and use an individualised transfusion decision. Hb130 is an optimisation/screening aim, not an RBC transfusion target.

## Evidence: populations and outcomes matter

TRICC supports a restrictive approach in many stable ICU adults; TRISS found no mortality advantage from a 90 versus 70 g/L trigger in septic shock, with fewer RBCs at 70. FOCUS did not improve its main functional/mortality outcome with routine Hb100 versus Hb80/symptoms after hip fracture. TRICS III supports a restrictive ≈75 trigger in its cardiac-surgery population; TITRe2's secondary mortality signal reminds us not to equate every trial/outcome. **MINT** in MI did not meet statistical superiority for the primary liberal-versus-restrictive comparison, but possible harm from restriction remained; **2025 AABB conditionally suggests a liberal strategy at Hb <100 g/L in AMI**, low-certainty evidence.

Acute brain injury is another exception to blanket generalisation: **TRAIN** found better neurological outcome with a 90 versus 70 trigger in its mixed brain-injury population; **HEMOTION** did not show statistically definitive primary neurological benefit of 100 versus 70 in moderate/severe TBI. **SAHARA** (2025 issue) did not establish primary neurological benefit of mandatory Hb≤100 versus optional Hb≤80 transfusion after aneurysmal SAH. Different populations, thresholds and endpoints mean these trials do not establish one universal neurocritical threshold. See R36 for the full comparison. Detailed neuroapplication remains in Set 6.

## Practical decision and implementation

For haemodynamically stable adults, **consider** RBCs below 70 g/L; ≈75 in cardiac surgery and 80 in orthopaedic/pre-existing cardiovascular disease are supported options. These are thresholds for consideration, not mandatory targets. Active haemorrhage, acute ischaemia, severe hypoxaemia, haemoglobinopathy and clinical intolerance need separate reasoning. In stable nonbleeding patients give one unit and reassess; do not wait for Hb70 during exsanguination or repeatedly transfuse to correct a number without investigating its cause.

Match plasma/platelets/fibrinogen to actual haemostatic need. Organise preadmission pathways, electronic support, bedside identification, transfusion consent, supply/traceability, TACO prevention and audit of patient outcomes and exposure/wastage. PREVENTT, neutral routine ANH and new TXA trials illustrate why physiological/Hb benefit is not automatically proven mortality benefit.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## PBM includes diagnostic blood loss and implementation

A 2026 BJA systematic comparison of international PBM guidance found particularly variable advice on reducing diagnostic blood loss and gaps in national coordination. That supports including minimum necessary sampling, appropriate small-volume tubes/closed sampling systems and a multidisciplinary implementation plan, rather than treating PBM as a transfusion-trigger number. Audit unnecessary samples, anaemia-treatment completion, transfusion appropriateness and patient outcomes. The review searched in March 2024: its 2026 publication date does not make it a synthesis of every 2025–2026 trial. [Primary abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42115060/) reviewed; no full-review claim.

## Anaemia definitions are not interchangeable with optimisation goals

The 2024 BJAEd corrigendum specifies the conventional adult WHO cut-offs of Hb <130 g/L for men and <120 g/L for nonpregnant women. Many perioperative PBM pathways use <130 g/L in either sex to trigger investigation/optimisation before major blood-loss surgery. Name the definition and population; neither number is an automatic transfusion target. [PBMCOR24](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534923001695)

## Self-marking checklist
- All three PBM pillars with pre/intra/post application
- Cause-based anaemia treatment without prophylactic Hb130 transfusion
- Accurate TRICC/TRISS/FOCUS/cardiac-trial scope
- MINT uncertainty plus current AMI guideline
- TRAIN versus HEMOTION without universal neuro threshold
- Stable thresholds versus active haemorrhage/physiological exceptions
- Single-unit reassessment, component selection and systems audit
- Includes diagnostic blood-loss reduction, implementation ownership and a publication-date/search-date distinction
- Separates conventional sex-specific anaemia definitions from perioperative Hb130 screening/optimisation

items.title: 21. Delayed compatible red cells in life-threatening bleeding
items.q: During life-threatening haemorrhage the blood bank reports that fully compatible red cells will be delayed because of antibodies. Describe your response and the distinction between alloantibodies and autoimmune crossmatch reactivity.
items.a:
## Coordinate lifesaving transfusion and haemostasis

Control the bleeding, activate/escalate the MHP and notify a **senior transfusion scientist/haematologist** of urgency, physiology and expected ongoing loss. Send correctly labelled pretransfusion samples and establish past antibodies, transfusions, pregnancy and special requirements. Consider salvage if appropriate/accepted. Do not wait for perfect serological compatibility while the patient exsanguinates; the blood bank selects emergency-release RBCs balancing immediate death against immunohaemolytic risk, with explicit clinician communication/documentation.

## Why compatibility is delayed

An **alloantibody** targets a nonself RBC antigen (e.g. K/E/Jk): clinically significant historical antibodies matter even if currently undetectable. Antigen-negative matched RBCs may take time to identify or obtain. Emergency group O prevents many ABO issues but **does not guarantee absence of the implicated non-ABO antigen**. RhD-negative/Kell considerations and childbearing potential matter, but critical stock/urgency requires specialist prioritisation.

A warm **autoantibody** can react broadly with patient/donor RBCs, making a completely nonreactive crossmatch impossible. The laboratory seeks underlying clinically significant alloantibodies using specialist methods and selects the best-matched product; do not withhold necessary blood until every auto-reactivity disappears or imply that the label “least incompatible” guarantees safety. Determine whether there is active haemolysis and treat its cause with haematology.

## Treatment-related test interference

Ask about **daratumumab/anti-CD38 therapy**: it can cause panreactivity in indirect antiglobulin testing and mask relevant alloantibodies. Notify the laboratory early and retrieve pretreatment phenotype/genotype where available; DTT-based methods can affect Kell antigen detection and influence component selection. Do not assume this pattern proves autoimmune haemolysis. See R35.

## Continue monitoring and transition

Check identity meticulously despite urgency, assess transfusion response, haemolysis, K/iCa/coagulation and organ perfusion, and communicate product/volume needs. Switch to group-specific and antigen-negative/compatible RBCs as soon as the blood bank advises. Record emergency authorisation, units and unresolved antibodies, explain the event to the patient when appropriate and preserve permanent antibody history for future care. Avoid ordering unnecessary plasma/platelets as a substitute for oxygen-carrying RBCs.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Immediate source control and senior blood-bank communication
- Correct samples/history and emergency authorisation
- No unsafe delay for complete compatibility in exsanguination
- Alloantibody antigen-negative selection and group O limitations
- Warm auto-reactivity versus masked alloantibody
- Monitors haemolysis/physiology and changes to ideal blood when feasible
- Documentation, disclosure and future antibody record

items.title: 22. Acute limb ischaemia after femoral arterial instrumentation
items.q: An ICU patient develops a cold, painful, pulseless leg after femoral arterial instrumentation. Outline your assessment and management, including the anticoagulation and reperfusion issues.
items.a:
## Treat as threatened acute limb ischaemia

Call vascular surgery immediately; note onset, instrument/procedure and embolic/thrombotic history. Examine both limbs for pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis and temperature; motor/sensory deficit signals threatened viability. Use Doppler, capillary perfusion and compartment examination, and assess systemic shock/other embolic sites. Analgesia, oxygen if needed, resuscitation and protect the limb from trauma/direct heating. Check access-site bleeding, anticoagulant exposure, AF, aortic disease, dissection, low-flow vasoconstriction and HIT timing.

## Prevent propagation and restore flow

Senior vascular/ICU decision on **IV UFH** promptly when not contraindicated; a recent intracranial/major bleed or suspected HIT changes the plan (nonheparin anticoagulant for HIT). Follow local dosing/assay protocol; do not choose a DOAC for an unstable patient needing imminent intervention. Limb duplex/CTA helps define occlusion if it will not delay reperfusion of an immediately threatened limb. Remove/reposition an implicated catheter only in coordination with the procedural/vascular team; avoid losing a useful route or provoking uncontrolled bleeding without a plan.

Revascularisation may use open embolectomy/thrombectomy, repair/bypass or catheter intervention according to viability/anatomy and timing. Catheter thrombolysis is unsuitable with major bleeding contraindications and not a substitute for immediate surgery in a severely threatened limb. An irreversibly ischaemic limb may require amputation; specialist classification determines this.

## Anticipate the anaesthetic and systemic effects

Account for full anticoagulation, blood loss, cardiac disease and neuraxial/deep-block contraindications. Reperfusion can produce **hyperkalaemia, acidosis, arrhythmia, vasoplegia, myoglobin-related AKI and compartment syndrome**. Check ECG, gas/K/iCa/renal function, prepare treatments and monitor urine/compartments; fasciotomy may be required. Plan ICU, ongoing anticoagulation by cause, secondary prevention and assessment of embolic source. Treating venous DVT pathways alone misses the urgency of arterial occlusion.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Prevention and catheter-related harm

The 2025 arterial-catheter review reinforces early recognition, prompt vascular input and prevention through ultrasound-guided placement, appropriate catheter size/site, minimal attempts and regular limb/site checks. A normal pre-insertion collateral test does not guarantee protection from subsequent ischaemia. Consider haematoma/compartment compression as well as intraluminal thrombosis. Routine addition of heparin to a flush has no established universal patency advantage and is inappropriate in suspected HIT; use the local line protocol. [ART25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534925000083)

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises limb threat and urgent vascular referral
- Examines viability, timing and instrument/embolic causes
- Anticoagulation with bleeding/HIT exceptions
- Imaging without delaying threatened-limb reperfusion
- Definitive open/catheter strategy and lysis limitations
- Anaesthetic anticoagulation constraints
- Reperfusion electrolyte/renal/compartment surveillance
- Links catheter-thrombosis recognition to prevention, compression complications and a safe flush strategy

items.title: 23. Anticoagulation in CRRT and ECMO; heparin resistance
items.q: Explain how anticoagulation differs between CRRT and ECMO, and how you would investigate apparent heparin resistance in an ICU patient.
items.a:
## Separate circuit patency from systemic thrombosis treatment

CRRT may use **regional citrate**: chelate calcium in the extracorporeal circuit, replace systemic calcium and monitor circuit/systemic iCa, acid-base, electrolytes and calcium requirements. It reduces systemic anticoagulant exposure; it does **not treat a concurrent DVT/arterial thrombosis**. Citrate accumulation is suggested by rising total:iCa **molar** ratio (often >2.5), increasing calcium requirements and metabolic disturbance; alkalosis may instead reflect metabolised citrate load. Severe shock/liver dysfunction requires careful protocol assessment, not a universal “always safe” or “absolutely prohibited” statement. UFH/no anticoagulation are selected alternatives when appropriate.

ECMO commonly uses **systemic UFH**, but flow, oxygenator/circuit clot, acquired vWF/platelet dysfunction, haemolysis and bleeding require an ECMO-specific protocol. Anti-Xa/APTT/ACT each have limitations; a single normal APTT is not proof of effective anticoagulation or safe haemostasis. HIT requires a nonheparin strategy, usually a specialist direct-thrombin inhibitor protocol with organ-function adjustment.

## Apparent heparin resistance

Check infusion delivery, line/sample problems, actual dose/weight and assay. High FVIII/fibrinogen in inflammation can shorten APTT, giving **pseudo-resistance despite therapeutic/high anti-Xa**; blindly escalating UFH may cause bleeding. Genuine low response can reflect antithrombin deficiency or increased binding/clearance. Compare APTT with appropriately interpreted anti-Xa, antithrombin if indicated, clinical/circuit thrombosis and laboratory limitations (haemolysis, bilirubin, residual Xa drugs). Antithrombin supplementation or changing agent is selected specialist management, not an automatic reaction to a low APTT.

## Ongoing assessment

Document the indication, systemic versus regional effect, target/assay and response. Review bleeding, platelet fall/HIT, renal/hepatic function, procedures and restarts daily. Recurrent circuit clot may be mechanical/flow-related and does not automatically mean insufficient systemic heparin. Detailed circuit prescriptions remain in the RRT/ECMO sets; this question tests the Set 2 anticoagulant decisions.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Separates regional citrate from systemic treatment
- Citrate/calcium/acid-base monitoring and accumulation clues
- ECMO systemic strategy and acquired haemostatic defects
- Checks delivery/sample/assay before escalating UFH
- Pseudo-resistance versus antithrombin-related resistance
- Uses multiple assays and clinical circuit/bleeding assessment
- Organ function, HIT and procedure/restart planning

items.title: 24. Isolated prolonged APTT with severe bleeding
items.q: A patient with new severe soft-tissue bleeding has an isolated prolonged APTT, normal PT and no previous bleeding history. Explain your diagnostic approach and immediate management.
items.a:
## Triage while investigating

Assess ABC/perfusion, bleeding source and Hb trend; call haematology early. Stop nonessential anticoagulants/traumatic procedures, obtain suitable access carefully and provide RBC/physiological support as required. An acquired factor VIII inhibitor is a dangerous possibility; other causes include heparin contamination/exposure, dabigatran, inherited VIII/IX/XI deficiency and lupus anticoagulant. Factor XII/contact deficiency can prolong APTT without clinical bleeding.

Repeat from a clean peripheral sample; review drugs, pregnancy/postpartum state, autoimmune disease and malignancy. Check FBC/platelets/film, fibrinogen, TT, relevant anti-Xa/dabigatran assay and haemolysis/organ tests as indicated. **Mixing study:** correction suggests deficiency; persistent or time-dependent prolongation suggests inhibitor. A delayed inhibitor effect requires incubated assessment; laboratory interpretation is essential. Send FVIII/IX/XI and inhibitor titre/Bethesda testing. Lupus anticoagulant often confers thrombosis risk and is not itself an explanation for this degree of haemorrhage.

## Treat suspected acquired haemophilia appropriately

For clinically significant bleeding, specialist haemostasis may require **rFVIIa, aPCC or recombinant porcine FVIII**, selected by disease/antibodies, monitoring and availability. FFP alone is usually inadequate against a significant inhibitor; normal VEM does not exclude it. Avoid assuming congenital-haemophilia replacement will work without an inhibitor assessment. Immunosuppression to eradicate the inhibitor is a separate specialist treatment, balancing infection risk. If emicizumab is involved, APTT/one-stage assays are misleading and aPCC combinations can cause TMA/thrombosis.

Monitor ongoing loss, Hb/perfusion and treatment response, minimise invasive/IM/neuraxial trauma, manage pain and plan monitored care. Do not wait for a final inhibitor titre to act on life-threatening bleeding with a strongly suggestive presentation.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises acquired inhibitor and immediate bleeding risk
- Excludes drug effect/contamination with clean sample
- Interprets immediate/incubated mixing study
- Sends factor/inhibitor testing and considers nonbleeding APTT causes
- Specialist haemostatic versus eradication treatment
- Explains FFP/VEM limitations and emicizumab caveat
- Avoids unnecessary trauma and monitors response

items.title: 25. Unexplained haemoglobin fall in ICU
items.q: An ICU patient has a progressive haemoglobin fall without obvious external bleeding. Outline your investigation and management, including when you would transfuse.
items.a:
## Confirm the fall and assess urgency

Repeat an unexpected result and check sampling dilution, Hb trend, fluids, transfusions and vital signs/perfusion. Shock, ischaemia or rapidly falling Hb warrants urgent source assessment/resuscitation; do not attribute it to “ICU anaemia” prematurely. Review surgery/drains, GI/urinary loss, puncture sites, retroperitoneal/abdominal bleeding, CRRT/ECMO circuit loss and repeated phlebotomy; image/endoscope according to findings and stability.

## Classify loss, destruction, dilution or low production

FBC/indices, reticulocytes and film organise the differential. Haemolysis: LDH/bilirubin/haptoglobin, DAT and urine; review transfusion timing, mechanical circuit/valve damage, drugs, G6PD triggers and TMA. Low/inappropriately normal reticulocytes: inflammation/hepcidin-mediated restriction, renal EPO deficiency, marrow suppression, nutritional deficiency or malignancy. Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; interpret TSAT/CRP and B12/folate selectively rather than automatically treating every high-ferritin inflammatory patient with iron. Check renal/liver function, coagulation and associated cytopenias.

## Treat the cause and preserve oxygen delivery

Control bleeding, stop causative drugs/circuit injury, treat sepsis/haemolysis and refer for unexplained pancytopenia/blasts. Minimise sampling, use small tubes and correct demonstrated deficiencies. Routine ESA for anaemia of critical illness is not supported simply to avoid a transfusion and can increase thrombosis. IV iron is not an immediate rescue for low oxygen delivery; weigh infection/indication and time to response.

RBC transfusion treats inadequate oxygen-carrying capacity: for many stable nonbleeding ICU adults consider Hb <70 g/L, one unit followed by reassessment. Acute MI, selected neurocritical states, severe hypoxaemia, ongoing haemorrhage and clinical intolerance require a different discussion. Do not use tachycardia/lactate alone to assume RBC deficiency when flow, infection or pain is the cause. Document response, TACO precautions and a durable cause-treatment plan.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Confirms trend/specimen and assesses instability
- Searches occult and iatrogenic blood loss
- Uses reticulocytes/film and haemolysis studies
- Evaluates inflammatory, renal, nutritional and marrow causes
- Treats cause and conserves diagnostic blood
- Qualifies stable threshold and key exceptions
- Single-unit reassessment and avoids automatic ESA/iron

items.title: 26. Platelets 45 in ICU: when to transfuse
items.q: An ICU patient has platelets 45 ×10⁹/L. Discuss your diagnostic approach and whether platelets are required for no procedure, a central venous catheter or major surgery.
items.a:
## Confirm and define the clinical problem

Review the film/repeat a citrate sample for clumping. Establish baseline, trajectory, timing of sepsis/CPB/heparin/new drugs, bleeding, thrombosis, fever, organ injury and other cell lines. Platelet function and anticoagulants matter independently of count. Causes: artefact, dilution, sepsis/DIC, HIT, immune drug-induced thrombocytopenia/ITP, TTP/HUS, marrow suppression/infiltration, hypersplenism and circuits. A fall with MAHA/neurological/renal injury needs urgent TMA assessment, while day-5–10 fall/thrombosis suggests HIT. Do not equate every low ICU count with DIC.

## Decide according to context

| Situation | Decision at 45 ×10⁹/L |
|---|---|
| Stable, no bleeding/procedure | Usually no prophylactic platelets; treat cause and trend. AABB 2025 uses <10 for many nonbleeding adult consumptive/hypoproliferative contexts, with important disease-specific exceptions |
| Ultrasound-guided compressible-site CVC | Not an automatic transfusion to 50. AABB conditionally recommends transfusion below 10; operator, site, function/drugs and local policy matter |
| Major nonneuraxial surgery | General guidance recommends transfusion below 50; coordinate timing/target and cause with the surgeon/haematologist |
| Intracranial/other critical-site bleeding | Higher individual targets often around 100; separate evidence and procedure-specific assessment |
| Diagnostic lumbar puncture | AABB recommends transfusion below 20, but this is **not a neuraxial anaesthesia/epidural threshold** |

## Cause-specific treatment and follow-up

TTP: urgent plasma exchange/specialist therapy, no routine prophylactic platelets. HIT: stop heparin, alternative anticoagulant; avoid routine platelets. ITP: immunomodulation, with platelets for serious bleeding/urgent intervention as part of the plan. DIC: cause control and components for bleeding/procedure, not isolated tests. Marrow suppression: disease-directed support and infection care. Recheck count/bleeding after transfusion, consider refractoriness and HLA/immune assessment if the increment is poor. Apply an individual VTE prevention plan as the platelet count recovers.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Worked delayed-transfusion pattern: post-transfusion purpura

If a patient's platelets fall profoundly with purpura/bleeding approximately 5–12 days after cellular-component transfusion, especially after previous pregnancy/transfusion, consider **post-transfusion purpura**. This is not the same as an immediate transfusion reaction, platelet refractoriness or red-cell hyperhaemolysis. An anamnestic recipient anti-HPA response causes destruction of donor and the patient's own platelets. Notify blood bank/haematology, investigate HPA antibodies and exclude competing causes. NZBS recommends IVIg **2 g/kg total in divided doses over 2–5 days**, with specialist monitoring. Avoid reflex repeated random-donor platelets; life-threatening bleeding can require urgently selected compatible/HPA-negative support. Record future component requirements. [PTPNZ](https://www.nzblood.co.nz/healthcare-professionals/transfusion-medicine/transfusion-medicine-handbook/7-adverse-effects-of-transfusion/7-10-post-transfusion-purpura)

## Thrombosis plus thrombocytopenia without the expected heparin history

With the appropriate adenoviral-vector vaccination history, severe thrombocytopenia, very high D-dimer, low fibrinogen and unusual-site thrombosis, consider **VITT** rather than assuming ITP. Send a PF4 ELISA and imaging directed by symptoms; a rapid HIT assay can be falsely negative. Treat a strong suspicion urgently with haematology while results are pending: IVIg plus a suitable non-heparin anticoagulant, with organ-function/bleeding assessment. ASH describes IVIg 1 g/kg daily for two days; use the specialist protocol. Avoid routine platelet transfusion, but catastrophic bleeding/urgent surgery requires an individual rescue decision. This is a historical exposure-linked differential, not a claim that all current vaccines cause VITT. [VITT](https://www.hematology.org/covid-19/vaccine-induced-immune-thrombotic-thrombocytopenia?s=09) [IVIG24](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534923001427)

## Self-marking checklist
- Confirms true count, timing and clinical phenotype
- Differentiates sepsis/DIC, HIT, TMA, ITP and production failure
- Applies modern no-procedure/CVC/major-surgery distinctions
- Separates LP from neuraxial anaesthesia
- Respects disease-specific platelet-transfusion cautions
- Reviews post-transfusion response and refractoriness
- Plans cause treatment and thrombosis prevention
- Recognises and treats post-transfusion purpura with appropriate HPA investigation/product planning
- Recognises exposure-linked VITT and distinguishes it from ITP, HIT and DIC

items.title: 27. Excessive bleeding with normal screening tests
items.q: A patient reports excessive bleeding after dental extraction and previous surgery. Platelet count, PT and APTT are normal. Describe your assessment, further investigations and perioperative plan.
items.a:
## Establish whether there is a clinically important bleeding phenotype

Clarify severity, timing and treatment of previous dental/surgical/obstetric bleeding, spontaneous bruising, epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding and deep haematomas/haemarthroses. Obtain old records and family history, including affected women/carriers. A structured bleeding-assessment tool can organise the history but does not replace judgment. Review aspirin/P2Y12 inhibitors, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, supplements, alcohol, renal/liver disease and connective-tissue features. Decide urgency and consequence of bleeding; refer to haematology before elective high-risk surgery.

## Explain what normal screening tests miss

Primary haemostasis involves platelet adhesion through VWF/GPIb, activation and GPIIb/IIIa-mediated aggregation. Secondary haemostasis generates thrombin and cross-linked fibrin. Mucocutaneous/immediate bleeding suggests platelet/VWF problems; deep or delayed bleeding suggests factor/clot-stability problems, but patterns overlap.

| Test/pattern | Interpretation and useful follow-up |
|---|---|
| Normal platelet count | Does not establish platelet function. Consider drug/uraemic dysfunction and inherited disorders; specialist aggregation/flow-cytometry testing may identify Glanzmann or other inherited phenotypes; Bernard–Soulier typically has large platelets with thrombocytopenia |
| Normal PT/APTT | Does not exclude vWD, mild VIII/IX/XI deficiency, factor XIII deficiency, platelet dysfunction or selected fibrinolytic disorders |
| Isolated prolonged PT | Consider warfarin/vitamin K, factor VII and early liver disease; assess medication and clinical context |
| Isolated prolonged APTT | Exclude contamination/drug effect, then VIII/IX/XI deficiency or inhibitor; contact-factor deficiency/lupus anticoagulant may not predict bleeding |
| Both prolonged | Assess DIC/dilution, liver disease, common-pathway defects or substantial anticoagulant effect |

Repeat appropriate samples and obtain blood film, fibrinogen, renal/liver tests, VWF antigen/activity and FVIII, with further factor, platelet or fibrinolysis testing directed by the phenotype. Mixing studies distinguish correction from persistent/time-dependent inhibition, with drug and laboratory caveats. Delayed bleeding with normal routine tests warrants consideration of FXIII/clot stability. FXI activity and APTT do not reliably predict procedural bleeding in isolation. Acquired VWF deficiency can accompany high-shear cardiac/mechanical-support or haematological disease. A normal VEM trace cannot clear these diagnoses.

## Translate less common diagnoses into treatment

Haemophilia B requires **FIX**, not FVIII, replacement under a factor-centre plan; DDAVP does not correct FIX deficiency. Inhibitors and prior allergic reactions change replacement/bypassing choices. For FXI deficiency, procedure and personal bleeding history matter as well as activity; selected mucosal procedures may use TXA, while major procedures may need plasma or a locally available specialist factor strategy, with thrombotic risk considered. Factor XIII deficiency needs a specific clot-stability diagnosis and appropriate replacement despite normal PT/APTT. Congenital fibrinogen deficiency/dysfunction needs quantitative and functional assessment and targeted replacement when indicated; some phenotypes also thrombose. Do not prescribe one generic factor concentrate for all rare disorders.

## Make a specific plan

Delay elective surgery when needed to define risk, with a written specialist treatment and rescue plan: adequate factor/VWF replacement, a tested appropriate DDAVP response, TXA where suitable, or platelet support for defined indications. Do not use DDAVP or plasma indiscriminately for every positive history. Some patients retain a bleeding disorder of unknown cause despite normal testing; their history still informs haemostatic planning. Specify products, monitoring, invasive/neuraxial precautions and delayed postoperative surveillance. Detailed haemophilia A and vWD worked plans remain in the SAQ bank.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Documents personal, procedural, family and medication history
- Explains primary versus secondary haemostasis and phenotype
- Recognises normal count/PT/APTT limitations
- Uses VWF/factor/platelet and clot-stability testing selectively
- Interprets mixing studies with drug/inhibitor caveats
- Does not equate normal VEM with safe haemostasis
- Coordinates a diagnosis-specific plan and delayed surveillance

items.title: 28. Thrombocytopenia, schistocytes and confusion in ICU
items.q: An ICU patient develops platelets 18 ×10⁹/L, anaemia with schistocytes and new confusion. PT is near normal. Discuss the differential diagnosis and immediate management.
items.a:
## Recognise a thrombotic microangiopathy without waiting for the full pentad

Thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic haemolysis and organ injury suggests TMA. Assess ABC, neurological/cardiac/renal injury, bleeding, blood pressure, infection, pregnancy/postpartum context, medicines, cancer and transplant history. Obtain film, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, creatinine/electrolytes, urine, coagulation/fibrinogen and ECG/troponin. Check previous Hb/platelets and exclude sampling artefacts. Involve haematology and ICU immediately.

| Possibility | Distinguishing considerations |
|---|---|
| Immune TTP | Severe ADAMTS13 deficiency/inhibitor; neurological/cardiac involvement can be prominent and renal injury varies. Normalish PT/APTT supports TMA but is not diagnostic |
| Shiga-toxin-associated HUS | Diarrhoeal/infectious context and renal injury; investigate with microbiology/nephrology |
| Complement-mediated HUS/TMA | Significant renal/systemic injury; exclude alternative causes and seek urgent specialist complement-directed assessment |
| DIC | Underlying sepsis/trauma/malignancy, falling platelets, high fibrin turnover and often prolonged PT/low or falling fibrinogen; early results can overlap |
| Other TMA/mimics | Severe hypertension, pregnancy-associated disease, drugs/transplant, mechanical haemolysis and malignancy; HIT is a different prothrombotic mechanism |

## Act urgently for suspected immune TTP

Send ADAMTS13 activity/inhibitor samples **before plasma treatment if feasible**, but do not delay treatment for results. A validated probability tool can help when testing is delayed. Arrange emergency therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids through an experienced centre; rituximab and caplacizumab are specialist additions. Caplacizumab limits VWF-mediated platelet microthrombosis; it does not eradicate the inhibitor and carries bleeding risk. Plasma infusion is not an equivalent definitive substitute for promptly accessible exchange in immune TTP.

Avoid routine prophylactic platelets in TTP; life-threatening bleeding or an indispensable procedure needs a joint decision. Give RBCs for clinical need and treat organ complications. Do not give heparin merely to “treat the microclots” or manage every TMA as DIC with repeated empirical components. Treat HUS/other TMA according to its cause rather than assuming every patient needs the same exchange regimen.

## Reassess diagnosis and response

Trend count, haemolysis and organ function, avoid unnecessary invasive procedures and document recovery/relapse follow-up. ISTH's 2025 update retains the acute immune-TTP treatment recommendations; its new recombinant ADAMTS13 recommendation concerns **congenital TTP**, principally replacement/prophylaxis, and must not be substituted for the immune-TTP pathway.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises TMA without requiring the classic pentad
- Differentiates TTP, HUS, DIC and important secondary causes
- Obtains ADAMTS13 before plasma when feasible without treatment delay
- Urgent plasma exchange plus corticosteroids for suspected immune TTP
- Explains specialist caplacizumab/rituximab roles and limits
- Avoids routine platelets and unjustified heparin
- Tracks organ injury and distinguishes congenital from immune TTP

items.title: 29. Delayed haemolysis after transfusion in sickle cell disease
items.q: A patient with sickle cell disease returns ten days after transfusion with pain, dark urine and haemoglobin below the pretransfusion value. Discuss your investigation and management.
items.a:
## Suspect delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction with hyperhaemolysis

An apparent pain crisis after transfusion can conceal destruction of donor and patient RBCs. Hb below the pretransfusion baseline is particularly concerning for hyperhaemolysis. Assess perfusion, oxygenation, chest symptoms, neurological findings and renal function; involve haematology and transfusion medicine urgently. Consider bleeding, infection, acute chest syndrome, aplasia, splenic sequestration and other haemolytic causes concurrently.

Send FBC/reticulocytes, film, bilirubin/LDH/haptoglobin, renal/electrolytes and urine. Obtain DAT, antibody screen and repeat compatibility testing, retrieving all historical antibodies and recent transfusion details. Follow HbA/HbS fractions where useful to identify rapid donor-cell disappearance. A negative DAT or current antibody screen does **not** exclude the reaction; antibodies may be evanescent or initially undetectable. Reticulocytes may be low relative to the patient's usual response.

## Avoid reflex transfusion while treating dangerous anaemia

Provide careful respiratory/perfusion support, analgesia and cause-directed treatment, avoiding fluid overload. Further RBCs can intensify hyperhaemolysis: do not automatically chase the previous Hb. Conversely, life-threatening anaemia may make transfusion necessary; make that decision jointly with haematology/blood bank, using extended antigen matching and a documented rescue plan. Do not delay lifesaving treatment to obtain a perfectly negative serological result.

ASH conditionally supports immunosuppression for ongoing hyperhaemolysis with very low-certainty evidence: specialist first-line therapy commonly involves IVIG and corticosteroids; eculizumab is a selected subsequent option. Rituximab may help prevent additional alloantibody formation when further transfusion is anticipated. These drugs have important adverse effects and need specialist protocols. Support erythropoiesis and correct demonstrable deficiencies; iron is not automatically appropriate in a chronically transfused patient.

## Monitor and prevent recurrence

Trend Hb, reticulocytes, haemolysis, renal function, oxygenation and treatment response. Record the reaction and all antibody history permanently, communicate future component requirements across institutions and explain warning symptoms to the patient. This is a delayed reaction, distinct from immediate ABO haemolysis and from routine postoperative anaemia.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises delayed haemolysis/hyperhaemolysis rather than pain alone
- Assesses competing diagnoses and organ injury
- Tests haemolysis, reticulocytes, antibodies and Hb fractions
- Understands negative DAT does not exclude the diagnosis
- Balances transfusion aggravation against life-threatening anaemia
- Specialist immunotherapy, matching and erythropoietic support
- Documents lifelong antibody/reaction history and follow-up

items.title: 30. Platelet refractoriness
items.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy remains severely thrombocytopenic after two platelet transfusions. Explain how you would investigate refractoriness and select further blood components.
items.a:
## Confirm the response and clinical urgency

Check bleeding, impending procedures and the actual indication for more platelets. Verify transfusion completion, dose/product, pretransfusion count and a count **10–60 minutes after completion**, ideally on two occasions. Exclude clumping or sampling/dilution artefacts. Ask the blood bank to calculate a corrected count increment using consistent units, body surface area and delivered platelet dose; a next-morning count alone cannot establish alloimmune failure.

## Separate consumption from alloimmunity

Nonimmune causes are common: ongoing bleeding, sepsis/fever, DIC, splenic sequestration, medicines and circuit consumption. A good early increment followed by a later fall suggests consumption, but timing patterns are not definitive. Poor early increments raise alloimmune destruction as a possibility, particularly after pregnancy or repeated transfusion. HLA class I antibodies are more common than HPA antibodies. Refractoriness and alloimmunisation are not synonyms.

Discuss HLA/HPA testing, platelet crossmatching and provision of selected compatible components with transfusion medicine. HLA-selected, antigen-compatible or crossmatch-compatible platelets are chosen by the demonstrated mechanism and availability; they are not a routine order for every low count. Treat nonimmune drivers. Continue necessary emergency haemostatic support during bleeding while optimal products are arranged; repeatedly giving unselected platelets to correct an isolated number can cause exposure without benefit.

## Specify what each product modification achieves

| Modification | Purpose and limits |
|---|---|
| Leukodepletion | Reduces donor leukocytes and some febrile/CMV/alloimmunisation risks; does not replace irradiation |
| Irradiation | Prevents donor-lymphocyte TA-GVHD for specific recipients/treatments/donations. NZ platelets are routinely irradiated; not every malignancy needs irradiated RBCs |
| Washing | Reduces residual plasma for selected severe allergic indications; not routine treatment of platelet alloimmunity |
| HLA/HPA selection | Addresses demonstrated alloimmune platelet destruction; requires advance planning and response checks |
| RBC antigen matching | Addresses RBC alloantibodies/haemoglobinopathy requirements; does not solve HLA-mediated platelet failure |

Confirm transplant/therapy-specific irradiated and CMV requirements with the blood bank. Recheck clinical haemostasis and early increments after selected products, documenting which intervention worked. Use disease-specific exceptions for TTP/HIT/ITP rather than applying chemotherapy prophylaxis thresholds to every patient.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Confirms true poor response on timed post-transfusion counts
- Uses correctly scaled CCI with blood-bank assistance
- Prioritises nonimmune consumption before assuming HLA antibodies
- Distinguishes HLA/HPA testing and compatible platelet options
- Treats bleeding and cause while products are arranged
- Distinguishes leukodepletion, irradiation, washing and matching
- Documents response and treatment-specific requirements

items.title: 31. Haemoglobinopathy groups and transfusion planning
items.q: Outline the major haemoglobinopathy groups and explain how their phenotype changes perioperative assessment and transfusion planning.
items.a:
## Classify the disorder before prescribing treatment

Haemoglobinopathies involve abnormal globin structure, reduced globin-chain production or combinations. Establish genotype, clinical severity, baseline Hb/reticulocytes, haemolysis, prior complications, current treatment and transfusion history. HPLC/electrophoresis and, where needed, molecular testing distinguish variants; recent donor transfusion can alter the measured fractions. Microcytosis alone is not proof of iron deficiency.

| Group | Clinical significance and anaesthetic implications |
|---|---|
| HbSS and sickle β⁰-thalassaemia | Often substantial haemolytic/vaso-occlusive disease; assess acute chest, stroke, pulmonary/cardiac/renal injury, pain and transfusion complications |
| HbSC and sickle β⁺-thalassaemia | Variable sickle disease; a higher baseline Hb does not imply negligible risk. Avoid an excessive viscosity rise from indiscriminate simple transfusion |
| Sickle trait | Usually asymptomatic; differs from SCD and does not justify routine preoperative exchange. Assess individual extreme physiological exposures and comorbidity |
| α/β-thalassaemia | Spectrum from trait to HbH/intermedia/transfusion-dependent disease. Severe forms require attention to ineffective erythropoiesis, organ effects, iron overload, antibodies and splenectomy risks |
| HbC/HbE | HbC disease can cause haemolysis; HbSC is a sickling disorder. HbE alone is often mild, but HbE/β-thalassaemia may cause severe or transfusion-dependent disease |

## Translate phenotype into a perioperative plan

Assess oxygen delivery and organ reserve rather than using a single generic Hb target. Severe thalassaemia may have iron-related cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, hepatic/endocrine disease and marrow-expansion/airway or skeletal changes. Investigate relevant organ effects, not every possible test in an asymptomatic carrier. Review chelation, chronic therapies and infection risk, including asplenia vaccination/fever precautions.

For SCD, avoid hypoxaemia, acidosis, hypothermia, dehydration, uncontrolled pain and excessive fluid. Plan postoperative respiratory care and VTE prevention. For significant haemoglobinopathy, coordinate antigen matching and all historical antibodies early; leukodepletion and irradiation address different risks. Simple versus exchange transfusion is individualised to baseline Hb, operation and disease severity, with hyperviscosity and previous delayed haemolysis considered. Routine HbS <30% or exchange is not required for every operation.

Treat proven coexisting deficiency, but do not routinely prescribe iron for thalassaemic microcytosis. G6PD deficiency is an enzymopathy, and methaemoglobinaemia a dyshemoglobinaemia; recognise them as related differentials rather than misclassifying them as a major inherited globin-chain group. The existing SCD/thalassaemia cases provide detailed disease-specific anaesthetic plans.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Separates structural variants from reduced-chain production
- Distinguishes sickle genotypes, disease and trait
- Covers α/β-thalassaemia and HbC/HbE combinations
- Uses phenotype and organ reserve rather than Hb alone
- Plans antibody matching and individual simple/exchange transfusion
- Avoids routine iron for microcytosis and universal HbS target
- Includes organ/airway, asplenia and postoperative risks

items.title: 32. Ooze after bypass: PCC versus plasma
items.q: A patient continues to ooze after cardiopulmonary bypass despite surgical haemostasis and adequate fibrinogen and platelets. Compare PCC and plasma, incorporating FARES-II and the limits of extrapolation to trauma.
items.a:
## Establish what deficit remains
