Reassess the surgical field and haemodynamics, temperature, ionised calcium, pH, sample quality and residual heparin/protamine effect. Review VEM and conventional tests alongside actual bleeding. Do not assume that a long CT/R means factor deficiency: low fibrinogen and anticoagulants can produce similar patterns. Verify the premise that fibrinogen and platelet contribution are adequate before adding thrombin-generating factors.

## Compare the products

Plasma supplies a broad set of soluble factors, including V and VIII, but requires a substantial volume, compatibility/logistical preparation and carries TACO/TRALI risks. Four-factor PCC provides concentrated vitamin-K-dependent factors with low volume and rapid administration, but does not replace fibrinogen, platelets or every plasma factor. Consider thrombosis and product-specific heparin/HIT cautions. Non-VKA use and dosing follow local approval/protocol; a favourable trial does not establish that every PCC formulation is interchangeable.

## Appraise FARES-II accurately

FARES-II (2025) randomised adults requiring coagulation-factor replacement for bleeding during cardiac surgery. Among the treated analysis population, haemostatic effectiveness was greater with PCC than frozen plasma and subsequent component exposure was lower. It met its prespecified noninferiority and superiority analyses for haemostatic effectiveness. This supports consideration of PCC in an appropriate post-CPB factor-deficiency algorithm; it is **not** evidence that every bleeding patient should receive empirical PCC. Review open-label treatment decisions, outcome definition, exclusions, product/dosing, setting, sponsorship and the limited ability to resolve uncommon thrombotic harm. A lack of a significant safety difference does not prove absence of risk.

## Distinguish other trials and apply the result

FIBRES addressed **fibrinogen concentrate versus cryoprecipitate** in a different deficit; PCC cannot replace either when fibrinogen is low. PROCOAG in trauma did not support routine empirical PCC and found increased thromboembolic events. The population, indication and timing differ from FARES-II, so neither trial cancels the other.

Select the product with the cardiac/transfusion team under the local algorithm, accounting for volume tolerance and the actual deficit. Reassess bleeding and tests after treatment and stop escalating once haemostasis is adequate. Detailed bypass conduct belongs in the cardiac set; the component-selection/evidence appraisal is retained here.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Additional current trauma evidence: FiiRST-2

**FiiRST-2 (2025)** compared early fibrinogen concentrate plus PCC with frozen plasma within a defined Canadian trauma major-haemorrhage strategy. It did **not** demonstrate superiority for 24-hour allogeneic component use and was stopped after an interim futility assessment. It tested a factor-concentrate replacement package, whereas PROCOAG tested empirical PCC added to usual trauma care and FARES-II tested cardiac-surgery factor replacement. These populations, comparisons and endpoints must not be collapsed into “PCC works” or “PCC never works”. No significant difference in a small trial is not proof of equivalence or exclusion of rare thrombotic harm. [FIIRST2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40982282/)

## Broader cardiac PBM context

The 2026 AHA cardiac-surgery PBM statement highlights preoperative anaemia/iron deficiency, intraoperative conservation, haemodilution and multidisciplinary planning. A post-CPB PCC-versus-plasma decision is one part of this pathway; it cannot compensate for untreated anaemia or replace surgical haemostasis. No new numeric recommendation is inferred from the abstract. [Primary abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42324995/) reviewed; the full statement was not reviewed here.

## New CABG review: preserve procedure-specific boundaries

The current in-press BJAEd CABG review reinforces anaemia investigation, minimising haemodilution, salvage and surgical haemostasis. Its elective cardiac P2Y12 timings are not neuraxial timings: for example, a surgical ticagrelor interval must not replace ASRA's longer neuraxial interval. Its broad bridging wording must not be exported to routine perioperative DOAC interruption; bridge only when the actual indication and guideline warrant it. Earlier ANH suggestions are interpreted alongside the newer neutral large cardiac trial already discussed in R16. [CABGPRESS](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X)

## Self-marking checklist
- Rechecks source, heparin, physiology and actual factor deficit
- Compares broad plasma replacement with concentrated PCC
- Explains what PCC cannot replace and its thrombotic/HIT risks
- States FARES-II population, comparison and efficacy direction
- Critiques design and uncertainty without inventing mortality benefit
- Separates FIBRES and PROCOAG populations/deficits
- Applies a local algorithm with reassessment rather than empirical PCC
- Places factor-product choice within preoperative and intraoperative cardiac PBM
- Does not export CABG interruption/bridging or older ANH statements into universal practice

items.title: 33. Whole blood versus components in trauma
items.q: Critically evaluate whole blood compared with component therapy for early major-trauma resuscitation, including the 2026 SWiFT and TOWAR trials.
items.a:
## Explain the proposed role

Whole blood can deliver oxygen-carrying cells and plasma together, with platelet contribution dependent on the actual collection, processing and storage product. It can simplify emergency delivery compared with multiple separately supplied components. Low-titre group O whole blood requires a specific blood-service policy: group O RBC compatibility does not make donor plasma universally harmless, and RhD/anti-A/anti-B exposure, cold chain, traceability, stock and wastage matter. Do not assume every product called whole blood has identical platelet content or equals a fixed adult component pack.

## Use the new randomised evidence

| Trial | Setting/comparison | Primary interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| SWiFT, 2026 | English air-ambulance services; up to two units of prehospital whole blood versus early RBC/plasma component care | Whole blood was not superior for the composite of death or massive transfusion within 24 hours |
| TOWAR, 2026 | North American air-medical cluster-randomised strategy; early low-titre group O whole blood versus components | No demonstrated reduction in 30-day mortality; account for cluster allocation and baseline imbalance |

These trials weaken a claim of proven superiority for **the tested limited prehospital strategies**. They do not prove equivalence, universal harm, or that all in-hospital, paediatric, obstetric and larger-dose whole-blood strategies have been settled. The comparator was early blood components, not a licence to delay blood while giving large crystalloid volumes. Trial product, dose, transport system and endpoints affect generalisability.

## Decide what to implement locally

Prioritise prompt haemorrhage control and timely blood within the local trauma/MHP system. Either selected whole-blood or component pathways need reliable supply, trained teams, patient identification, warming, ionised calcium monitoring and serial haemostatic assessment. Whole blood does not remove later needs for targeted platelets/fibrinogen or drug reversal. Assess operational benefits, donor constraints, emergency compatibility and monitoring, as well as trial outcomes, before changing stock policy.

The NZ SWiFT Aotearoa feasibility work compares locally relevant products and must not be confused with the completed English SWiFT effectiveness trial. Detailed prehospital trauma systems belong in the trauma set; the blood-product comparison and recent evidence belong here.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Defines whole-blood rationale and product variation
- Explains emergency ABO/RhD and logistical considerations
- Correct SWiFT comparison and composite outcome
- Correct TOWAR setting and mortality interpretation
- Distinguishes no demonstrated superiority from equivalence/harm
- No extrapolation to every population or unlimited dose
- Links local implementation to source control and targeted ongoing care

items.title: 34. Stable suspected pulmonary embolism: agent and duration
items.q: A postoperative patient develops unilateral leg swelling and possible pulmonary embolism but is haemodynamically stable. Outline diagnosis and treatment, including agent choice and duration.
items.a:
## Establish probability and identify deterioration

Assess vitals, oxygen requirement, chest symptoms, perfusion and bleeding; shock or RV failure requires the existing high-risk-PE pathway. Consider oedema, haematoma, infection and venous obstruction as alternative causes of leg swelling. Use a validated pretest-probability pathway in the appropriate population; postoperative D-dimer is often raised and cannot diagnose VTE. Obtain proximal compression ultrasound for suspected DVT and CTPA for appropriate suspected PE, using V/Q or alternative strategies when contrast/imaging is unsuitable. Negative testing may require serial/further imaging when suspicion remains high.

If imaging is delayed, interim therapeutic anticoagulation is a probability-versus-bleeding decision, especially immediately after surgery. Check Hb/platelets, renal/liver function, coagulation, drugs, neuraxial catheter status and the operation's haemostatic consequences. A prophylactic dose is not adequate treatment of a confirmed proximal DVT/PE.

## Choose treatment for this patient

Anticoagulation is usual treatment for proximal DVT and most PE; routine thrombolysis is inappropriate for stable uncomplicated VTE. Select an approved DOAC or parenteral agent according to absorption, renal function, bleeding, interactions and procedural needs. Apixaban/rivaroxaban have initial higher-dose treatment phases; dabigatran/edoxaban require initial parenteral treatment. Follow current local availability and drug-specific prescribing rather than using a maintenance dose from day one.

LMWH is often useful while unstable oral intake or cancer-related considerations are clarified; UFH may be selected for severe renal impairment or rapidly changing procedural/reversal needs. Active GI/GU cancer, thrombocytopenia and drug interactions affect DOAC suitability. High-risk antiphospholipid syndrome favours specialist VKA-based treatment rather than routine DOAC use. A neuraxial catheter requires a safe removal/restart plan before therapeutic anticoagulation. Reassess confirmed isolated distal DVT separately: selected low-risk cases may have serial imaging, while symptoms/extension risk favour treatment.

## Duration, exceptions and follow-up

Treat a surgery-provoked proximal DVT/PE for at least three months in most cases, then reassess recurrence and bleeding risks. Unprovoked, recurrent or persistent cancer-related VTE may warrant longer therapy; the duration is not determined solely by the postoperative label. IVC filters are reserved for selected genuine anticoagulation contraindications, with a retrieval plan. Limb-threatening venous occlusion requires urgent specialist rescue.

Document transition, adherence, bleeding advice, planned procedures and follow-up. Do not perform indiscriminate thrombophilia testing during acute illness/anticoagulation or assume a family history automatically changes treatment.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Uses probability and appropriate ultrasound/PE imaging
- Does not diagnose postoperative VTE from D-dimer alone
- Balances interim treatment against fresh surgical bleeding
- Distinguishes treatment from prophylaxis and drug initiation phases
- Adjusts agent for renal function, cancer, APS and procedures
- Plans duration/reassessment and limited filter indications
- Recognises high-risk PE, distal-DVT and limb-threat exceptions

items.title: 35. Haematological emergencies in leukaemia, lymphoma and myeloma
items.q: Describe the haematological emergencies that may alter the immediate anaesthetic plan in a patient with leukaemia, lymphoma or myeloma.
items.a:
## Recognise time-critical disease beyond a low blood count

Assess clinical urgency, disease/treatment status, infection, organ reserve, bleeding/thrombosis, airway/mediastinal compression and the reason for surgery. Call haematology early. FBC/film, clotting/fibrinogen, blood gas, renal/electrolytes, calcium/phosphate, urate and LDH are directed by the suspected emergency. Treat sepsis, shock, hypoxaemia and major bleeding concurrently; avoid a generic anaesthetic plan before identifying the dominant risk.

| Emergency | Immediate implications |
|---|---|
| Suspected APL with coagulopathy | Bleeding and thrombosis can be catastrophic. Haematology-led **ATRA should begin on suspicion**, without waiting for molecular confirmation; support platelets/fibrinogen/plasma and avoid nonessential invasive procedures. Do not use routine TXA/heparin or leukapheresis as generic treatment |
| Hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis | Respiratory/neurological dysfunction can be an emergency even without a universal WCC cutoff. Urgent cytoreduction and careful fluid/metabolic support; RBC transfusion may worsen viscosity, so coordinate essential transfusion rather than chasing a normal Hb |
| Tumour lysis | Hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, secondary hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and AKI can precede or follow treatment. Monitor ECG/serial biochemistry and urine; treat dangerous hyperkalaemia, use specialist urate-lowering therapy and renal support when indicated |
| Hyperviscosity/paraproteinaemia | Visual/neurological symptoms and mucosal bleeding require specialist assessment, sometimes urgent plasma exchange; coordinate transfusion and volume strategy rather than increasing viscosity indiscriminately |
| Neutropenic sepsis | Immediate antibiotics/source control with appropriate haemodynamic support; an apparently mild fever may be serious |

## Distinguish treatment hazards and prepare safely

For tumour-lysis prevention/treatment, prescribe fluids to actual cardiac/renal tolerance with close reassessment. Rasburicase lowers existing urate; allopurinol prevents new urate formation. Check G6PD before rasburicase and avoid it in deficiency. Routine urine alkalinisation is not recommended. Isolated asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in severe hyperphosphataemia is managed differently from symptomatic arrhythmia/seizure: involve renal/haematology rather than automatic repeated calcium replacement.

Myeloma also raises concerns about renal injury, hypercalcaemia, infection and fragile bones. Daratumumab can interfere with indirect antiglobulin compatibility testing; inform the blood bank early, retrieve pretreatment phenotype/genotype where available and let the laboratory use validated methods. DTT can obscure Kell antigens, changing product selection. This is not necessarily a new alloantibody or active haemolysis.

Coordinate haemostatic targets, invasive access, ICU and rescue resources; defer nonessential procedures until the immediate emergency is treated. Detailed malignancy therapy and mediastinal-mass anaesthesia remain in their specialist sets; this answer tests the haematological problems that change today's plan.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Worked treatment-related deterioration: CAR-T

Ask about recent CAR-T therapy and contact the treating centre immediately when fever, hypoxia, hypotension or neurological change develops. **Cytokine-release syndrome (CRS)** can produce vasodilatory shock and respiratory failure; infection, tumour lysis and other causes may coexist. Provide cultures and prompt indicated antimicrobials, cautious fluid reassessment, oxygen/ventilation and vasopressors as needed. Treat CRS under the current centre grading/pathway, commonly with IL-6 receptor blockade (tocilizumab), with steroids or additional immunomodulation when indicated; do not withhold necessary rescue solely from fear of impairing cancer therapy.

**ICANS** may present with inattention, aphasia, altered handwriting, confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness, with or without simultaneous CRS. Record a baseline/serial ICE assessment, check glucose/electrolytes and exclude haemorrhage, infection and nonconvulsive seizures; obtain urgent neurological/ICU input, EEG and imaging as indicated. Corticosteroids are central to significant ICANS treatment. Tocilizumab is used for associated CRS, **not as the sole treatment of isolated ICANS**. Secure the airway and manage seizures/cerebral oedema when necessary. Cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinaemia and later infections also matter after CAR-T. Immune-effector-cell-associated HLH-like deterioration needs the specialist team's separate assessment; not every high ferritin after CAR-T is interchangeable with CRS. [CART22](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534922000701) [HLH25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924001264)

## Self-marking checklist
- Identifies the dominant haematological emergency before induction
- APL: urgent specialist ATRA and haemostatic support
- Leukostasis/viscosity and cautious necessary RBC transfusion
- Recognises and manages tumour-lysis metabolic/renal risk
- Rasburicase/G6PD and no routine alkalinisation
- Recognises sepsis, paraprotein and myeloma organ risks
- Communicates anti-CD38 compatibility interference and procedure timing
- Recognises CAR-T CRS/ICANS, treats possible sepsis concurrently and uses the treating centre pathway
- Does not use tocilizumab alone for isolated ICANS; monitors neurological deterioration and cytopenias

items.title: 36. Red-cell thresholds in ICU, myocardial infarction and brain injury
items.q: Evaluate red-cell transfusion thresholds in stable general ICU patients, acute myocardial infarction and acute brain injury. Explain why a single restrictive threshold is insufficient.
items.a:
## Start with oxygen delivery and the clinical setting

Hb-bound oxygen dominates arterial oxygen content, but delivery also depends on saturation and cardiac output. Blood loss, low flow and hypoxaemia require correction alongside Hb. Establish whether the patient is actively bleeding, stable but anaemic, ischaemic or unable to compensate; identify transfusion harms including TACO. An initially normal Hb can conceal acute whole-blood loss. Threshold trials in stable patients do not justify waiting during exsanguination.

| Population | Evidence-informed interpretation |
|---|---|
| Stable general ICU/sepsis | TRICC/TRISS support restrictive strategies in their populations; a consideration threshold around 70 g/L is commonly appropriate, with symptoms and physiology considered |
| Cardiac/orthopaedic or stable cardiovascular disease | AABB-supported options include about 75 g/L for cardiac surgery and 80 g/L for orthopaedic/pre-existing cardiovascular disease; these are not universal postoperative targets |
| Acute MI | MINT did not demonstrate statistically definitive superiority for its primary comparison, but harm from restriction could not be excluded. The 2025 AABB AMI guideline conditionally favours a liberal strategy below 100 g/L, with low-certainty evidence |
| Mixed acute brain injury | TRAIN compared approximately 90 versus 70 g/L and favoured the liberal strategy for its neurological outcome; do not assume all brain injuries share its effect |
| Moderate/severe TBI | HEMOTION compared approximately 100 versus 70 g/L and did not establish a statistically definitive primary neurological benefit; this is not proof of equivalence |
| Aneurysmal SAH | SAHARA, published in issue in 2025, compared mandatory transfusion at ≤100 with optional transfusion at ≤80 g/L. Its primary 12-month neurological result did not show significant benefit of the liberal strategy |

## Critically compare rather than vote-counting trials

Different injury types, transfusion protocols, comparator thresholds, outcome definitions, follow-up and uncertainty explain why “liberal neurotransfusion works/does not work” is too crude. No significant difference is not equivalent to demonstrated equivalence. Evaluate the patient's ongoing ischaemia, cardiac reserve, oxygenation, cerebral context, bleeding and overload risk with the responsible ICU/neuro/cardiac team. Do not extrapolate an acute-MI recommendation to every patient with old coronary disease.

## Prescribe and reassess

For stable nonbleeding adults, consider one RBC unit then reassess symptoms, Hb and physiology rather than automatically ordering two units. Treat the underlying anaemia, reduce phlebotomy and document the indication/target. Major haemorrhage uses a separate resuscitation strategy; haemoglobinopathies and chronic transfusion programmes also need disease-specific plans. Detailed cerebral perfusion management belongs in Set 6, while the comparison of transfusion evidence is covered here.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

## Self-marking checklist
- Uses delivery, bleeding and symptoms rather than Hb alone
- States stable ICU and selected surgical thresholds with scope
- Accurate MINT uncertainty and conditional 2025 AMI guidance
- Differentiates TRAIN, HEMOTION and SAHARA populations/protocols
- Distinguishes nonsignificance from equivalence
- Individualises ischaemia/organ reserve versus TACO risk
- Single-unit reassessment and cause-based anaemia care

items.title: 37. Non-factor prophylaxis in haemophilia before major surgery
items.q: A patient with haemophilia receiving non-factor prophylaxis is booked for major surgery. The APTT is normal. Compare the implications of emicizumab, antithrombin-lowering treatment and anti-TFPI therapy for assessment, haemostatic cover and laboratory monitoring.
items.a:
## Identify the treatment before interpreting the test

Obtain the haemophilia-centre plan, diagnosis (A or B), baseline severity, inhibitor status, exact agent, last dose, prior bleeding/thrombosis and the proposed operation. Non-factor prophylaxis changes haemostasis without necessarily replacing FVIII/FIX. A normal APTT does **not** prove normal factor activity or adequate major-surgery cover. Do not interrupt an unfamiliar long-acting drug or add high-dose factor/bypassing agents empirically: coordinate the specialist perioperative and rescue plans well ahead of elective surgery.

## Compare the mechanisms

| Treatment family | Mechanism and implications |
|---|---|
| **Emicizumab** | Bispecific antibody that bridges FIXa/FX and mimics part of FVIIIa cofactor activity in haemophilia A; it does not treat haemophilia B or eradicate a FVIII inhibitor |
| **Fitusiran** | Antithrombin-directed siRNA lowers antithrombin synthesis and increases thrombin generation; a rebalancing strategy for haemophilia A/B, with or without inhibitors in its US approval |
| **Anti-TFPI agents** (for example concizumab/marstacimab) | Reduce tissue-factor-pathway-inhibitor activity to rebalance coagulation; exact approved population, breakthrough-bleed treatment and monitoring are product-specific |

Availability and approval differ by country; a US label is evidence of a therapy and its safety requirements, not a claim that it is funded or stocked locally. These are prophylactic strategies, not universal acute surgical reversal products.

## Laboratory interpretation and major-surgery cover

Emicizumab markedly shortens APTT and invalidates many APTT-based FVIII/inhibitor measurements. Use an appropriately validated **bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII assay** and inhibitor testing when indicated, with the laboratory aware of the drug. One-stage FVIII results must not be used to declare major surgery protected. Major surgery usually still requires factor or bypassing cover, selected by inhibitor status and the written centre plan. In an emicizumab-treated inhibitor patient, **rFVIIa is generally preferred to aPCC**, because aPCC exposure can cause TMA/thrombosis; the drug-specific rescue policy remains essential.

For antithrombin-lowering and anti-TFPI agents, conventional clotting tests are not a general validated perioperative target. Fitusiran uses scheduled antithrombin-activity monitoring under its label and requires special breakthrough-bleed/surgery guidance; over-treatment with conventional factor/bypassing regimens can cause thrombosis. Its 2025 US approval carries major warnings for thrombotic events and gallbladder disease, with hepatic monitoring. Do not copy a historical fixed trial dose or extrapolate an emicizumab assay/rescue rule to every rebalancing drug. [FITUSIRAN](https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/219019s000lbl.pdf)

## Integrate the anaesthetic plan and follow-up

Use an experienced centre and confirm access to the chosen haemostatic products, assays and rescue team before incision. Plan atraumatic airway/vascular techniques, conservative regional decisions, surgical haemostasis, appropriate TXA where suitable, normothermia and postoperative analgesia/rehabilitation. A normal APTT is not clearance for a neuraxial catheter. Monitor actual bleeding, Hb and appropriate specialist assays, as well as thrombotic/TMA features, renal dysfunction and drug-specific adverse effects. Document which tests are unreliable and who controls rescue dosing at every transfer. Treatment innovation improves prophylaxis but does not remove the need for an individual major-surgery haemostatic plan. [WFH](https://www1.wfh.org/publication/files/pdf-1863.pdf) [BLEED25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12597351/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Establishes A/B phenotype, inhibitor status, exact drug and centre plan
- Distinguishes factor mimicry from antithrombin/TFPI rebalancing
- Explains why a normal APTT does not prove major-surgery protection
- Uses validated bovine chromogenic/inhibitor assays with emicizumab
- Plans factor/bypassing cover and emicizumab/aPCC risk appropriately
- Recognises fitusiran drug-specific monitoring and thrombotic/gallbladder/hepatic risks
- Does not assume foreign licensing equals local availability
- Provides safe technique, postoperative monitoring and clear rescue/assay handover

items.title: 38. Febrile ICU patient with cytopenias and ferritin 18,000 (HLH)
items.q: An ICU patient remains febrile with progressive cytopenias, ferritin 18,000 micrograms/L, falling fibrinogen and organ dysfunction despite appropriate sepsis treatment. Discuss the diagnosis, investigations and immediate management.
items.a:
## Recognise hyperinflammation while continuing resuscitation

Suspect secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH): persistent fever, falling blood counts and markedly raised ferritin with evolving organ injury. Uncontrolled immune activation can drive marrow suppression, hepatitis, hypofibrinogenaemia and shock. Sepsis, DIC and HLH can coexist. Continue appropriate infection treatment and organ support; apparent antibiotic resistance is a reason to reconsider the diagnosis, not to stop antimicrobials automatically. Involve ICU, haematology and rheumatology/infectious diseases urgently. [HLH25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924001264)

## Establish probability and competing diagnoses

Review the trajectory, drug/exposure history, immune disease, malignancy, recent chemotherapy/CAR-T/transplant and infection clues. Examine for organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, bleeding, neurological and cardiac dysfunction. Ferritin is not diagnostic: liver injury, infection, iron loading and malignancy also raise it. A very high or rapidly rising value increases concern in this clinical pattern. Repeat FBC/film, ferritin, coagulation/fibrinogen, triglycerides, renal/liver tests and LDH; assess haemolysis, gas/lactate and organ-specific markers. Consider marrow failure, TMA, drug effects and other causes of cytopenias. [HIHASC](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38258680/)

Use **HScore** to support probability, not as a stand-alone confirmatory test or gatekeeper to treatment. Its components include immunosuppression, temperature, organomegaly, number of cytopenic lines, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen, AST and marrow haemophagocytosis. **HLH-2004** conventionally uses a compatible molecular diagnosis or five of eight features: fever, splenomegaly, cytopenias in at least two lines, high triglycerides and/or low fibrinogen, haemophagocytosis, low/absent NK activity, raised ferritin and raised soluble CD25. It was developed in a different population, some tests return slowly, and meeting the formal research-derived rule must not become a prerequisite for treating a rapidly deteriorating adult. [Original HLH-2004 guideline abstract](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16937360/). Bone-marrow haemophagocytosis may be absent early and can occur in other critical illnesses; neither its absence nor presence settles the diagnosis. Obtain specialised immune tests with the laboratory/specialist team when useful. [HLH25](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S2058534924001264)

## Investigate triggers in parallel

Send cultures and directed viral/microbiological tests, including EBV/CMV/HIV where indicated; obtain imaging for occult infection, lymphoma or organomegaly when safe. Retrieve pretreatment samples where practical. Seek tissue/marrow diagnosis if malignancy is suspected, ideally before steroids if this can be achieved promptly without unsafe delay. Infection, haematological malignancy and autoimmune/autoinflammatory disease are major trigger groups, and more than one can be present. [HIHASC](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38258680/)

## Start specialist treatment before a prolonged diagnostic search is complete

Progressive probable HLH may require immunomodulation while investigations continue. EULAR/ACR supports context-dependent high-dose glucocorticoids, anakinra and/or IVIg; these are not a mandatory fixed sequence for every trigger. The team selects formulation, dose and route according to organ involvement, renal function, infection and diagnostic concerns. Selected severe/refractory or malignancy-associated cases require etoposide-based or other directed therapy. Do not delay lifesaving treatment merely to obtain marrow haemophagocytosis or every specialist result. Treat the trigger concurrently. [EULARHLH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11040593/)

## Monitor response and complications

Support circulation, oxygenation, renal function and haemostasis according to physiology and actual bleeding/procedural needs. Trend cell counts, ferritin, fibrinogen, liver/renal function and organ support; investigate failure to improve rather than escalating blindly. Monitor immunosuppression complications and arrange appropriate prophylaxis, nutrition and follow-up. Improvement does not remove the need to identify occult lymphoma/infection or plan relapse surveillance. [EULARHLH](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11040593/)

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises fever, falling counts and high ferritin as an HLH warning pattern
- Allows coexistence with sepsis/DIC and continues indicated antimicrobial/supportive care
- Uses trends, organ assessment, triglycerides/fibrinogen and appropriate differential diagnosis
- Treats HScore/HLH-2004 as supportive tools rather than infallible tests
- Does not require marrow haemophagocytosis or treat ferritin alone as diagnostic
- Searches for infection, malignancy and autoimmune triggers in parallel
- Plans urgent specialist immunomodulation without a fixed universal regimen
- Monitors response, treatment harm, occult triggers and relapse

items.title: 2025.2 Q5: Point-of-care testing in acute haemorrhage
items.q: Evaluate point-of-care testing modalities used in the management of acute intraoperative haemorrhage.
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Evaluate several modalities and their limitations in acute haemorrhage rather than describing ROTEM alone.

## Why point-of-care testing (POCT)

Conventional PT/APTT/fibrinogen testing assesses selected plasma pathways; platelet count is a separate cellular test. Laboratory turnaround varies and may lag rapid bleeding. Early VEM amplitudes and blood gases are often available within minutes, supporting targeted decisions; a complete VEM/lysis assessment takes longer.

## Modalities

**Viscoelastic tests (TEG, ROTEM, Sonoclot, ClotPro)**
- Basis: whole-blood clot formation measured over time (clotting time, clot kinetics, maximum clot firmness, lysis).
- Advantages: assess selected components of **whole-blood clot initiation, strength and lysis under low shear**, without reproducing the whole in-vivo haemostatic system (factors, fibrinogen, platelets, fibrinolysis); rapid early amplitude values (A5/A10) guide therapy; can reduce component use when integrated into validated bleeding algorithms, with evidence differing by setting; detect **hyperfibrinolysis** (and so guide tranexamic acid).
- Limitations: do not assess **platelet function** well (without platelet mapping), von Willebrand disease or the effect of antiplatelet drugs; insensitive to some **anticoagulants** (some DOACs) and typically run at 37°C, so may conceal the patient's hypothermic impairment; do not assume a normal trace excludes physiological or unmeasured defects; variability between machines and reagents; sample handling and operator error; good evidence in cardiac and liver surgery but **weaker in trauma and obstetrics**; need training and quality control.

**Platelet function tests (multiplate, VerifyNow, TEG platelet mapping)**: assess antiplatelet drug effect and platelet contribution; limited by thrombocytopenia, haematocrit and by being a snapshot; uncertain correlation with bleeding.

**Activated clotting time (ACT)**: heparin monitoring for bypass and vascular surgery; **non-specific**, affected by hypothermia, haemodilution and platelet count.

**Point-of-care INR/PT/aPTT**: selected coagulation endpoints measured by platform-specific methods; many devices use whole blood but report a plasma-pathway result. Accuracy and validation may be limited outside their intended anticoagulant-monitoring use, particularly in shock, low haematocrit and extreme results.

**Blood gas analysers**: **haemoglobin, ionised calcium, lactate, pH and potassium** guide transfusion and calcium therapy; no coagulation information alone.

**Fibrinogen assays (functional fibrinogen from viscoelastic tests)**: key because fibrinogen is the first factor to fall; the Clauss method lab result is slow.

## Evaluation

Viscoelastic-guided algorithms reduce blood product use and probably bleeding in cardiac surgery, but mortality benefit is unproven and **trials in trauma (ITACTIC) were inconclusive**. POCT works best with a **local algorithm**, regular quality assurance, and clinical judgement; no single test addresses all components, so combine viscoelastic testing, platelet testing as indicated, blood gas and clinical findings.
rubric: Rationale: speed and goal-directed therapy compared with laboratory tests
Viscoelastic tests: basis, advantages and limitations
Platelet function and ACT testing described
Blood gas parameters (haemoglobin, calcium, lactate) as POCT
Specific limitations (platelets, DOACs, hypothermia, sample handling)
Combines tests within a local algorithm

items.title: 2025.1 Q5: Major transfusion reactions under general anaesthesia
items.q: Outline the diagnosis and management of major transfusion reactions during general anaesthesia.
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Recognise major reactions during anaesthesia, discriminate their features and provide reaction-specific management; lengthy generic anaphylaxis detail alone does not address the breadth.

## Context

Under anaesthesia, the usual warning symptoms (fever, rigors, pain, dyspnoea) are masked. Diagnosis rests on **unexplained cardiovascular or respiratory change, bleeding, haemoglobinuria, or rash** during or soon after a transfusion.

## Types and diagnosis

- **Acute haemolytic reaction (ABO incompatibility)**: hypotension, tachycardia, **diffuse oozing (DIC)**, haemoglobinuria (red or brown urine), raised temperature, bronchospasm. Check the bag against the patient; send blood for repeat crossmatch, direct antiglobulin test, free haemoglobin, bilirubin, LDH, coagulation, and urine.
- **Anaphylaxis (multiple mechanisms; anti-IgA in selected patients)**: hypotension, bronchospasm, urticaria, angioedema; tryptase.
- **TRALI**: acute hypoxaemia and **bilateral pulmonary infiltrates** within 6 hours, permeability oedema without hydrostatic overload as the main explanation. Coexisting cardiac disease and mixed TRALI/TACO are possible; filling pressure/BNP alone does not decide.
- **TACO**: hypertension, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema, positive fluid balance; high BNP; improves with diuresis.
- **Bacterial contamination/sepsis** (platelets especially): fever, hypotension, rigors, positive cultures.
- **Febrile non-haemolytic reaction** (mild), **hyperkalaemia**, **hypocalcaemia** with rapid transfusion, hypothermia.
- Differentials: drug anaphylaxis, sepsis, surgical haemorrhage, embolism.

## Management

- **1.** **Stop the transfusion**, keep the bag and giving set; **maintain IV access with a fresh set/line and 0.9% saline**; do not flush the implicated blood into the patient or restart a unit implicated in a major reaction.
- **2.** Call for help, 100% oxygen, secure airway, and **resuscitate by ABC**.
- **3.** **Check identity** (patient, bag, compatibility) and call the **blood bank/transfusion service** to investigate and quarantine blood.
- **4.** **Supportive therapy**: fluids, vasopressors (adrenaline for anaphylaxis), restore renal perfusion and monitor urine/electrolytes; avoid indiscriminate fluid loading or forced mannitol/diuresis as a substitute for treating shock (diuretics only for a justified indication after assessment), treat DIC with products guided by viscoelastic tests, treat hyperkalaemia, ventilate (TRALI: lung-protective), diuretics for TACO.
- **5.** **Antibiotics** (broad-spectrum) for suspected bacterial contamination, cultures of patient and product.
- **6.** **Monitor in ICU/HDU**, renal function, and complete incident reporting/haemovigilance and **disclosure**.
rubric: Discriminating features (haemolysis, TRALI, TACO, anaphylaxis, sepsis)
Stop transfusion and keep the bag
Communication with blood bank and identity check

items.title: 2024.2 Q10: Intraoperative cell salvage: circuit, indications and drawbacks
items.q: Outline the functional elements of an intraoperative cell salvage system. (30%) Discuss the indications, advantages and disadvantages of intraoperative cell salvage. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Describe functional elements accurately and evaluate indications, benefits and limitations.

## Collection, processing and administration

Use trained staff, a separate salvage suction circuit and a clearly identified patient. Anticoagulant (heparinised IV-grade saline or citrate at the manufacturer's specified concentration/rate) mixes with shed blood; low suction, commonly −100 to −150 mmHg, and aspiration from a pool limit haemolysis. The collection reservoir filters gross debris. Swab washing may recover cells using IV-grade isotonic saline; avoid hypotonic irrigation fluid.

A centrifuge separates cells by density. Discard supernatant and wash the red cells with IV-grade 0.9% saline according to the device programme, removing most anticoagulant, free Hb, plasma and contaminants. Return a labelled **washed RBC suspension**, commonly haematocrit around 50–70%, through an appropriate administration filter. This supplies essentially **no platelets or clotting factors**. Follow the device/local expiry; the BJAEd review recommends reinfusion within **6 h of first collection**, rather than applying the allogeneic 4-hour rule to every salvage system. Do not pressurise the salvage bag or force blood through a leucocyte-depletion filter: air embolism, bag rupture and hypotension are risks.

## Indications and benefits

Consider collection when anticipated loss exceeds **500 mL or 10% blood volume**, with processing governed by yield and economics: major vascular/cardiac, revision orthopaedic/spinal, trauma and selected obstetric/oncological operations. Particularly useful with rare antibodies or accepted alternatives to donor blood. Reduced allogeneic exposure conserves stock and avoids some donor-related hazards. Cells retain oxygen-carrying function without a donor storage period; this does not guarantee better survival or eliminate every transfusion risk. Initial set-up does not mean processed blood is immediately available in exsanguination.

## Limitations and contamination decisions

Equipment, disposables, staff training, quality assurance and sufficient case volume determine value. Haemolysis, identification error, hypothermia, air embolism, residual contamination, and reinfusion hypotension—especially with some leucocyte filters—can occur. Large-volume RBC-only salvage still requires haemostatic component and calcium monitoring.

Divert suction away from faeces, urine, gross pus, chlorhexidine/iodine, topical haemostatic agents and unset bone cement. **Sepsis and malignancy are not absolute contraindications**: use individual risk assessment, careful collection/washing and selected filtration; filters do not guarantee sterility or removal of all malignant cells. Routine irradiation of salvaged cancer blood is not a universal requirement. Obstetric use requires a specific protocol; leucocyte-depletion filters are not universally mandatory and can impede rapid flow/cause hypotension. RhD-negative unsensitised mothers with RhD-positive infants need assessment for fetomaternal haemorrhage and anti-D under local policy. Sickle disease/trait and thalassaemia require specialist consideration of sickling/fragility. Obtain individual consent, including whether a continuous circuit or swab washing is accepted.

> **Evidence anchor:** See the current source register for the applicable review depth and links; historical examiner expectations and contemporary clinical guidance are distinguished.

Centrifugation, IV-grade isotonic washing and labelled reinfusion

items.title: 2022.2 Q5: Haemophilia A for total knee replacement
items.q: A 56-year-old male with haemophilia A is scheduled to undergo a total knee replacement. Describe the pathogenesis of haemophilia A and its complications. (50%) Discuss how the presence of haemophilia A influences your perioperative management of this patient. (50%)
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Explain FVIII deficiency/inheritance and apply a coordinated perioperative factor/inhibitor plan to knee replacement.

## Pathogenesis and complications (50%)

**Haemophilia A** is an **X-linked recessive deficiency (or dysfunction) of factor VIII**, causing failure of the intrinsic tenase complex (FIXa, FVIIIa) and impaired thrombin generation, so clots are unstable and slow. It affects males, with female carriers variably affected. **Severity by factor VIII level**: severe (under 1%), moderate (1 to 5%), mild (5 to 40%). Coagulation tests: typically **prolonged aPTT, normal PT and platelets**, but mild disease can have a normal aPTT. Factor assays establish activity; emicizumab can normalise aPTT despite severe endogenous FVIII deficiency.
**Complications**
- **Haemarthrosis** (knee, elbow, ankle) leading to **haemophilic arthropathy**, synovitis and joint destruction (the reason for the knee replacement).
- Muscle haematoma, **intracranial haemorrhage**, airway and retroperitoneal bleeding.
- **Inhibitors** (alloantibodies to FVIII, 20 to 30% in severe disease), **blood-borne viruses** (hepatitis C and HIV from older plasma products), and renal and chronic pain problems.

## Perioperative management (50%)

- **Major centre** with a haemophilia team; **multidisciplinary plan with haematology** well in advance.
- **Preoperative**: FVIII level and **inhibitor screen**, FBC and group and screen, viral status, liver function; plan recombinant factor VIII (or extended half-life product, or emicizumab with adjunct as directed); optimise Hb.
- **Factor replacement**: raise FVIII to **80 to 100% before surgery**, then maintain a specialist-defined peak/trough plan (WFH higher-dose **peak** examples: **60–80% days 1–3, 40–60% days 4–6, 30–50% days 7–14**) including rehabilitation; give by **bolus or continuous infusion**, **measure levels** (pre, post, daily). If inhibitors exist, select specialist factor/bypassing treatment. In an emicizumab-treated inhibitor patient, **rFVIIa is preferred over aPCC/FEIBA** because of TMA/thrombosis risk; use validated bovine-reagent chromogenic FVIII/inhibitor assays. Emicizumab alone is not adequate cover for major surgery.
- **Adjuncts**: **tranexamic acid** (IV, with caution in renal bleeding), desmopressin in mild disease, and meticulous surgical haemostasis; **avoid IM injections** and NSAIDs.
- **Anaesthesia**: GA is usual; **neuraxial/regional blocks are risky** unless factor levels are normal and the haematologist agrees; use ultrasound and fine needles for peripheral blocks; **avoid nasal intubation**, gentle laryngoscopy, and take care with positioning and tourniquet.
- **Blood management**: assess physiological tolerance of anaemia, use appropriate transfusion thresholds, consider salvage only with appropriate selection, and use tranexamic acid, and anticipate **postoperative bleeding**.
- **Postoperative**: HDU, continued factor cover, multimodal analgesia (no NSAIDs), thromboprophylaxis (mechanical, individualised), and rehabilitation planning.
rubric: Factor VIII deficiency, X-linked, severity classification
Surgery in a major centre with haematology input
Factor VIII replacement with targets, timing and level monitoring
Tranexamic acid and avoidance of NSAIDs and IM injections

items.title: 2021.1 Q14: Warfarin for atrial fibrillation: perioperative anticoagulation
items.q: Discuss the options for anticoagulation management in the perioperative period for a patient taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation who requires a laparotomy for ischaemic bowel.
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Provide a patient-specific perioperative plan and urgent warfarin reversal, balancing bleeding and embolic risks.

## Overview

This is **emergency surgery**, so there is no time for the usual 5-day interruption. The priority is **rapid reversal of warfarin** while weighing the **embolic risk** (the likely cause of the ischaemia) against **surgical bleeding**.

## Preoperative

- **Assess urgency** (resuscitate, antibiotics, and proceed within hours), the last INR, last dose, and the indication: **AF with prior embolism** is high risk; CHA2DS2-VASc score.
- **Reversal**:
  - **Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC)** 25 to 50 units/kg (INR-based) **plus vitamin K 5 to 10 mg IV** (slow). PCC acts within minutes, IV vitamin K begins sustained correction over several hours but maintains the effect.
  - FFP is slower and large-volume (volume overload); use only if PCC is unavailable.
  - Aim for INR **below 1.5** (neuraxial placement needs normalised INR under the relevant guideline and is inappropriate during this unstable urgent scenario).
- Weigh vitamin K dose: high doses can make later re-anticoagulation difficult, but at this stage safety comes first.

## Intraoperative

- **Plan for bleeding**: arterial line, large-bore access, blood available, viscoelastic testing, TXA only for an appropriate bleeding indication rather than automatically in ischaemic bowel, selected cell salvage, and normothermia.
- Avoid regional/neuraxial block unless INR is normal; use **TAP/rectus sheath** only with caution.

## Postoperative

- **Restart anticoagulation early** once haemostasis is secure (timing individualised to haemostasis, bowel/vascular findings and ongoing embolic risk; therapeutic treatment after major surgery may need ≥48–72 h or longer), after evaluating the actual embolic cause/risk; if a true ongoing high-risk embolic indication requires therapeutic treatment while nil by mouth, titratable IV UFH may be selected once bleeding allows. Do not automatically bridge AF or prescribe a fixed UFH-to-LMWH sequence. Restart warfarin and any overlap only under the agreed specialist plan; give ordinary VTE prophylaxis separately when safe.
- ICU monitoring for bleeding, re-ischaemia, and renal function; involve haematology/surgeons.
rubric: Balance of embolic risk versus bleeding
Reversal with PCC and vitamin K (doses and INR target)
Individualises postoperative anticoagulation, route and timing; no automatic therapeutic bridge

items.title: 2019.2 Q11: Rivaroxaban in a patient on a transplant waiting list
items.q: A patient on an organ transplantation waiting list is taking rivaroxaban for recurrent pulmonary emboli. Discuss your perioperative anticoagulation plan.
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Plan before the unpredictable transplant call, apply rivaroxaban pharmacology and tailor decisions to the organ, renal function and urgency.

## Key issues

- **High thrombotic risk** (recurrent PE) with **unpredictable timing** of a **high-bleeding-risk** operation (organ transplantation), so the transplant is effectively elective until the call, then urgent.
- **Rivaroxaban**: direct factor Xa inhibitor, peak 2 to 4 hours, **half-life 5 to 9 hours (up to 11 to 13 hours in the elderly)**, about **one-third renally cleared**; **no routine INR-based monitoring**; normal PT/APTT cannot exclude relevant activity. A drug-calibrated anti-Xa assay is preferred when quantification will change an urgent decision.

## Planning (in consultation)

Multidisciplinary plan with **transplant team, haematology and anaesthesia** well before the call.

**At listing (stable phase)**
- Consider a transplant-specific **alternative maintenance strategy**: selected LMWH with renal adjustment, or warfarin because INR is measurable and rapid reversal is available; warfarin is not short-acting. IV UFH is a short-acting, titratable inpatient option when justified, not routine chronic outpatient therapy. The organ, anticipated call interval, renal function and thrombotic risk determine the plan with haematology.
- If rivaroxaban continues, maintain a written call-in plan and a reliable last-dose record; ask and verify the time rather than assuming it is unknown.

**At the call (urgent surgery)**
- **Ask the time of the last dose**, renal function, weight, and perform an anti-Xa level if available.
- If surgery cannot wait (usually transplant ischaemic times are limited), **delay induction where feasible** towards a drug/renal-function-specific low residual level (routine high-bleeding-risk interruption is usually longer than 12–24 h; organ ischaemic time may preclude waiting) or use **reversal**: specialist-directed **4-factor PCC (often 25–50 IU/kg under protocol)** if clinically indicated. Do not present andexanet as routine preoperative reversal: indications/availability are restricted, thrombosis is a major concern, and it can cause heparin unresponsiveness if CPB is required. US sales ended in December 2025 after an FDA safety review; this does not establish NZ availability. Activated charcoal is an early-ingestion option with airway protection, usually within about 2 h; later use is drug-specific specialist advice.
- Plan for **bleeding**: viscoelastic testing, blood products, tranexamic acid, cell salvage; avoid neuraxial block.

**Postoperative**
- Restart anticoagulation early at therapeutic dose once bleeding allows (usually ≥48–72 h after high-bleeding-risk surgery, and only when haemostasis permits); use **UFH or LMWH** initially because of renal graft function, drug interactions (calcineurin inhibitors) and the flexibility needed.
rubric: Recognises high thrombotic risk and high bleeding risk surgery
Considers a transplant-specific alternative maintenance/call-up strategy; no routine DOAC bridge
Time of last dose and urgent options at the call
Indication-specific PCC/reversal decisions, andexanet safety/access limits and early charcoal caveats
Bleeding plan and avoidance of neuraxial block
Postoperative restart with renal and drug interaction awareness

items.title: 2019.1 Q10: Microcytic anaemia before revision hip replacement
items.q: These are the blood results of a 65-year-old man scheduled for a revision total hip replacement. Hb 120 g/L (130-165), MCV 78 fL (80-100), WCC 5.5, Plt 250, Na 136, K 4.0, Urea 5.5, Cr 100. Iron 8 µmol/L (5-30), transferrin 3.2 g/L (2.0-3.2), transferrin saturation 12% (10-45), ferritin 40 µg/L (25-300), C-reactive protein 8.0 mg/L (0-5). Interpret these results. (30%) How would you manage this patient preoperatively? (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Interpret the results in context and investigate the underlying anaemia rather than offering treatment alone.

## Interpretation (30%)

- **Mild microcytic anaemia** (Hb 120, MCV 78) in a man.
- **Iron studies**: low-normal iron and **transferrin saturation 12% (low for assessment of iron availability)**, **ferritin 40, not reassuring in this inflammatory/microcytic context**. With **CRP mildly raised**, ferritin (an acute-phase protein) is falsely elevated, so **iron deficiency cannot be excluded**: a ferritin under 100 µg/L with TSAT under 20% in inflammation is consistent with **absolute or functional iron deficiency** (mixed with anaemia of chronic inflammation from the arthritic/failed joint).
- Normal white cells and platelets, and no major biochemical renal abnormality evident, but creatinine 100 alone does not establish normal CrCl/eGFR in a 65-year-old.
- **Differential for microcytosis**: iron deficiency (including **occult gastrointestinal blood loss**, especially in a 65-year-old man), anaemia of chronic disease, thalassaemia trait, sideroblastic anaemia.

## Preoperative management (70%)

- **1.** **Investigate the cause**: history (melaena, weight loss, NSAIDs, diet), examination, appropriate referral for **GI investigation (endoscopy/colonoscopy)**; a negative stool-blood test must not be used to exclude the source or delay indicated investigation since a man of this age with iron deficiency needs a source; consider B12/folate, reticulocytes, haemoglobin electrophoresis if indicated.
- **2.** **Treat the anaemia** (patient blood management): **IV iron** (a locally available formulation dosed to calculated deficit, body weight and product limits) is preferred if oral iron is ineffective, not tolerated, or surgery is within 4 to 6 weeks (oral iron about 40–60 mg elemental daily or 80–100 mg on alternate days, according to formulation/tolerance); recheck Hb in 2 to 4 weeks; erythropoietin only in selected cases.
- **3.** **Timing**: revision hip surgery has high blood loss (often 1 to 2 litres), so discuss deferring elective surgery for investigation/optimisation; **130 g/L is an optimisation aim, not a universal cancellation or transfusion target**.
- **4.** **Blood loss minimisation**: tranexamic acid, cell salvage, normothermia, restrictive transfusion triggers, group and screen with crossmatch, and review of antiplatelets and anticoagulants.
- **5.** **Other optimisation**: cardiovascular assessment, and stop NSAIDs where possible.

> **Current evidence:** PREVENTT did not show lower transfusion/death with preoperative IV iron in its anaemic major-abdominal-surgery population. Treat demonstrated deficiency, investigate its cause and monitor response without promising a universal transfusion or survival benefit. IV iron risks include hypersensitivity, extravasation staining and formulation-related hypophosphataemia.
rubric: Interprets Hb, MCV and iron studies in the context of raised CRP
Identifies likely iron deficiency or mixed anaemia
Investigates the cause (occult GI loss) in a man of 65
Iron therapy (oral versus IV) and recheck

items.title: 2019.1 Q13: Family history of von Willebrand disease
items.q: Outline your approach to the perioperative management of a patient who gives a strong family history of von Willebrand disease.
items.model:
> **Examiner feedback (summary):** Establish personal/family bleeding phenotype, investigate vWD and plan treatment according to response, subtype and procedure.

## Overview

Von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the **commonest inherited bleeding disorder** (laboratory low-VWF phenotypes are more prevalent than clinically significant diagnosed disease), autosomal, due to deficiency or dysfunction of **von Willebrand factor (VWF)**, which mediates platelet adhesion and carries factor VIII. Presentation: mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, easy bruising, postpartum haemorrhage), and surgical bleeding.

## Confirm the diagnosis

- **History**: personal bleeding (dental extraction, surgery, menstrual, postpartum), drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs, anticoagulants), and a structured bleeding score.
- **Tests**: FBC, **aPTT** (may be prolonged), PT; **VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor/GPIbM), factor VIII**, VWF multimers, blood group (group O has lower VWF); repeat testing, because levels vary with stress, pregnancy, exercise and oestrogen.
- **Types**: **Type 1** (partial quantitative deficiency; most common, mild), **Type 2** (qualitative: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), **Type 3** (virtually absent VWF, severe).
- **Refer to haematology** well before elective surgery.

## Management

- **Responders (mostly type 1)**: **desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 micrograms/kg IV** over 30 minutes, an hour before surgery (VWF and FVIII rise 2- to 5-fold), after a **test dose** with levels. Limit to 24 to 48 hours (**tachyphylaxis**); **fluid restriction and sodium monitoring** (hyponatraemia, seizures); caution in the elderly, ischaemic heart disease, and children under 2 years.
- **Non-responders, severe/type 3 disease, most type 2 disease, or major surgery** (selected type 2 responders require specialist testing; DDAVP must not be sole major-surgery cover): **VWF/FVIII concentrate** (e.g. Biostate, Wilate), aiming for **VWF activity and FVIII above 50 to 100%** before surgery and both **VWF activity and FVIII ≥0.50 IU/mL for at least 3 days** after major surgery, extended according to procedure/bleeding risk and serial trough levels. **Type 2B**: desmopressin is contraindicated (thrombocytopenia). Platelets in Type 3 with alloantibodies.
- **Adjuncts**: **tranexamic acid** (also as mouthwash), local haemostasis, avoid NSAIDs/aspirin, and for menorrhagia hormonal therapy.
- **Anaesthesia**: neuraxial/deep blocks require an individualised haemostasis plan, adequate VWF **and FVIII**, no additional coagulopathy and a safe catheter-removal/maintenance plan with haematology; one value above 50% is not a universal clearance; avoid nasal intubation, IM injections; take care with laryngoscopy.
- **Postoperative**: monitor for bleeding for several days, continue prophylaxis, and plan follow-up.
rubric: History, family history and bleeding scores
Regional anaesthesia criteria and postoperative monitoring
